I place these figures on Hansard because I feel there are many people in all parts of the maritimes who would like to see them, particularly in view of the fact that many newspapers have carried different sets of figures which in most cases were incorrect.
I wish to speak now about another industry in Northumberland county, the Christmas tree industry. Christmas trees to the approximate value of $325,000 were shipped to United States by rail and highway from Chatham, Newcastle and adjacent points on the Miramichi. This industry, a seasonal one, operates during the months of October, November and December and plays an important part in the economy of Northumberland. By proper cutting and rotation the small fir trees that grow on the Miramichi can furnish the Christmas tree markets for years to come, from which can be derived substantial revenues.
The year 1952 being the largest export season for pitwood and pulpwood in the life of the Miramichi, together with the long lumber and the fishing industries, the Christmas tree industry and large-scale defence construction programs of millions of dollars, with other phases of industry and business enjoying an accelerated pace, resulted in Northumberland reaching its peak year.

The present outlook for 1953 points to a drop in quantity and per cord price of pitwood for the U.K. market. Scandinavian prices for pit-props have been reduced and at the present time the U.K. inventories are substantial. It is anticipated that the United Kingdom will place a fair volume of pit-prop contracts with eastern Canada for 1953 shipment. Present indications are that quantities will be considerably lower than the 1952 shipments. It is also anticipated that France and Turkey will take a volume of pit-props during 1953. The United Kingdom's experience in 1950 in depending solely upon European sources should be a deterrent which should make her hesitate to again withdraw from the Canadian market.
I am sure that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and his officials, particularly Canada's trade commissioner in London, are doing everything within their power to secure the largest possible order from the United Kingdom for 1953 purchases of pit-props as well as from other countries.
While it is appreciated that this industry is of a free enterprise nature, the trade and those connected with it, from the woods to the wharves, can feel sure that every assistance is being rendered by the federal government.
The long lumber demand from Miramichi producers is at present normal. Early orders for 1953 requirements are being received, and while the price is down about $10 a standard it is hoped that overseas, United States and domestic demands will keep this industry on an even keel during 1953. The defence construction program in the Miramichi area is expected to be very substantial in 1953. This of course depends on the international situation. Other industries and business generally are expected to maintain the 1952 level.
I should like to ask members of the house, and particularly the members of the cabinet, to seriously consider the problems of the maritimes in the light of future existence and the necessity of industrial expansion. The constituency of Northumberland, New Brunswick, through which flows the historic and important Miramichi river, a shipping lane for ocean-going vessels of the largest types, like other parts of the maritimes, forms a part of this great Canada of ours. In it the descendants of the English, French, Scottish and Irish pioneers live in perfect harmony side by side, resolved, individually and collectively, to make Canada a still greater nation and to foster national unity in a true Canadian spirit.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what Canada makes makes Canada.

What Canada produces produces Canada. Blessed is the country that can, and does, make and produce its own. Such a nation, wisely governed, is beholden to no man and to no combination of men.
On December 4, as recorded at pages 339 to 344 of Hansard,, I discussed the matter of the Canadian beet sugar industry as it relates to national defence. It is my purpose today to consider the question of the Canadian sugar beet growing industry as an eminently respectable branch of farm business in Canada.
Sugar beets are grown in soil and generally on farms. There can be no doubt that sugar beet raising is a farming enterprise. True, the sugar beets are processed in a sugar factory before their product, sugar, becomes available to supply human needs. But wool growing requires a processing factory to render available yarn, cloth and clothing. Wheat growing requires a mill to produce flour. Generally vegetables and small fruits go through a canning factory to produce canned goods. Milk is often processed-in creameries to become butter, or in the cheese factories to become cheese.
Therefore I maintain that, notwithstanding the fact that sugar beet growing depends for its welfare upon the sugar factory, there can be no doubt whatever that sugar beet growing is a branch of Canadian agriculture. Sugar beet raising has an unchallengeable right to a recognized place and a respected and even honoured membership in the splendid sisterhood of Canadian agricultural industries. Therefore I contend that no man or group of men has any right to kick the sugar beet industry around as though it were a noaccount cur that amounted to nothing. Sugar beet raising in Canada has by past achievement merited, and should freely be accorded, full title to a standard equal to that of grain growing, fruit growing, potato growing, dairying, fur farming, meat raising, sheep raising, tobacco growing, soya bean growing and the rest of them-and I may say that in the case of nearly all these products the constituency of Lethbridge, Alberta, is famous for its achievements.
Sugar beet raising is a branch of agriculture and therefore has an incontestable right to be exempt from all forms of discrimination from which other branches of agriculture are exempted. It has a complete right to be entitled to all forms of assistance to which other branches of agriculture are entitled, and that without reservation or question. Is there any conceivable reason why sugar beet growing should not, for example, come under the Agricultural Prices Support Act? While we are on the matter, how would you feel about 68108-54
The Address-Mr. Blackmore the consistency of a nation that would put an agricultural price support under a given commodity and then let in vast quantities of that same commodity from another nation, thus destroying its domestic production?
First let it be known without qualification that beet sugar, the major end product of the sugar beet, is in every respect exactly the same as the finest cane sugar. There are still people spreading lies around Canada that beet sugar is somehow or other inferior to cane sugar. These people are either deceived or they are downright hypocritical. Let me read a passage to support the statement I have just made. The United States department of agriculture, bureau of chemistry and soils, says:
It is not possible to chemically differentiate cane sugar and beet sugar by the physical appearance of the two sugars, and there is no evidence to show that cane sugar is sweeter than beet sugar or vice versa. It has been alleged at times that beet sugar has an unfavourable effect in making jelly and preserves. It has been stated, for instance, that beet sugar prevents jellying. The bureau of chemistry has conducted experiments in the manufacture of apple and grape jelly, using commercial granulated beet sugar and commercial granulated cane sugar under identical conditions. As a result of these experiments, no difference was found to exist in the finished products in any of their characteristics, and no difference could be detected between jellies made with beet sugar and those made with cane sugar. In all probability the failure to produce the desired jellying effect, which has been observed at times, has been due to such factors as deficiency of pectin in the fruit juice, absence of proper acidity, etc. The highest grades of granulated sugar on the market reach an ideal state of purity so far as all practical purposes are concerned, and it is believed that where the highest grades of commercial granulated sugar are used there is no choice between beet and cane sugar.
It would be in the interests of Canada if the government would issue a statement similar to the one I have just read from the United States government. How can a country be wisely governed and well informed when people are deluded by misstatements?
The sugar beet is a king amongst vegetables. The average sugar beet is from ten to twelve inches long, it weighs from 1J to 2 pounds, it is light in colour, something like a parsnip. I am taking some care to go into detail in the matter because I realize that a good many members in the house have never seen a sugar beet and there are certainly millions of people in Canada who have not seen one.
Sugar beets have yielded as high as 23 tons to an acre, a colossal per acre yield. A good average crop is 12 tons per acre which, in itself, is an enormous yield. A good sugar beet, if well bred and well cared for in good soil with enough water and sunshine, will carry a high percentage of sugar-as

The Address-Mr. Blackmore high as 16 to 18 per cent or more. That percentage stands among the very top achievements in the world. The average sugar content in Alberta sugar beets over the past twenty years has bordered closely upon 17 per cent.
Canadian land where sugar beets are now grown has good soil, adequate sunshine and water. Canadian irrigated lands are especially blessed in all three of these respects. The sugar beet is one of the surest props-one of the great anxieties in agricultural industries is the uncertainty of the crop, but sugar beets are almost a certain crop under most conditions.
No disease comparable to rust in wheat, or smut in grains, or blight in potatoes, remains unconquered in Canadian sugar beets. No insect pest comparable to the wheat-stem saw-fly, the corn borer and various kinds of weevil, is uncontrolled in sugar beets. Sugar beets, growing, are successfully resistant to slight frost, frost which would normally come during their period of growth. Sugar beets in summer have a fair chance of recovering from hail-which is again an important matter. The average Canadian fall weather does not prevent the harvest, or harm the beets seriously after harvest. Beet harvesting, usually, comes after the garnering of most farm crops and consequently the work of gathering sugar beets is economical in the farm schedule of yearly activity.
Sugar beets have a sure market in Canada if governmental wisdom preserves it for them. It ought to be recognized ordinarily, and I believe it is by all realistic persons, that it is proper for the producers of the country to have the first right to the market of that country. Sugar beet growers are assured of a fair cash price because the farmers and beet processors sign contracts, before seeding begins-guaranteeing the beet raisers an attractive initial payment on the beets when delivered, and participation in returns from sales of the sugar and by-products as the sales are made.
How well do sugar beets yield in Canada? The average tonnage per acre from 1925 to 1950 in Alberta was good. It was rarely lower than 12 tons to the acre. The average sugar content percentage through the same years was, generally speaking, good. Very rarely did it fall below 16 per cent and several times it went above 18 per cent. The average sugar yield per ton in Alberta is good, as compared with sugar beets in almost any part of the world.
The sugar beet is a king and a queen amongst vegetables in respect of the by-products that it yields Canadians. Someone has


said that if a sugar beet could squeal we would utilize even the squeal. That is how completely the sugar beet is used.
May we consider these by-products and what they mean in terms of nutrients for livestock? According to the fifteenth report and financial statement of the Alberta cooperative sugar beet growers, a very reliable organization in point of accuracy of knowledge, "in meat production the various byproducts alone from an average acre of beets, not counting sugar, produces as much meat as will the product of an average acre of corn." Now that is a most important fact.
While primarily it might be said that we raise sugar beets to produce sugar, yet in raising sugar beets we are producing per acre a crop of nutrients-animal food-equivalent to what could be raised if you were raising on that acre almost any forage crop that can be named, and raising it for forage alone.
There are four by-products. They are beet tops, beet pulp, beet molasses, and beet tailings. Now, what are beet tops? Those who have had experience with raising beets know that the upward part of the beet, probably to an inch to an inch and a half below the base of the leaves, does not contain sugar and may contain undesirable elements which can mar the value of the sugar. Consequently the upper inch or inch and a half is cut off when the beets are harvested. Thus we see there are left all the leaves and the upper portion of the beet itself. Those portions remain on the field or are gathered up and hauled in to be treated as any other kind of valuable nutrient would be treated. They constitute what is called beet tops.
How valuable are those beet tops? Silver Sunshine, the 1946 fall issue, at page 31, tells us that tops from the average ton of beet contain approximately 200 pounds of dry matter. This according to 27 experiments conducted throughout the western United States in 1943, will replace 100 pounds of alfalfa hay and 46 pounds of grain in fattening cattle and sheep. One hundred pounds of beet tops therefore equal 50 pounds of alfalfa hay and 23 pounds of grain. Now, a rapid computation of the figures I have given will readily enable any ordinary member to estimate just how much nutrient value there is in beet tops from a 12 ton crop.
What is the value of beet tops? Beet tops from an average 12 ton crop are worth $19.50 per acre as feed when alfalfa hay is $14 per ton and barley is 60 cents a bushel. Tops cured and well dried will replace grain at the rate of one pound of tops for half a pound of grain. This is all authenticated and vouched for in the periodical, Silver Sunshine, to which I have referred.

The Canada and Dominion Sugar Company, at page 49 of its submission to the tariff board in 1939, reference 106, quoted from reports of the statistical branch of the Ontario department of agriculture to the effect that the past five-year average yield of alfalfa, per acre in Ontario, was 2-32 tons.
Then the report says "so that a sugar beet grower gets on an average about two-thirds as much value in stock feed from his beet tops as if he had cropped his land solely to alfalfa hay".
"Beet tops properly siloed are worth as much as the beets". So says the Silver Sunshine periodical in the fall of 1946, at page 10.
I have shown that one ton of beets will yield 200 pounds of dried beet tops, equal to 100 pounds of alfalfa hay and 46 pounds of grain. A 12 ton beet crop will yield 12 times 200 pounds or 2,400 pounds of dried beet tops equalling 1,200 pounds of alfalfa hay and 552 pounds of grain. Silver Sunshine in the spring of 1948, at page 22, says: "Livestock prefer beet top silage above all other feeds".
It must be obvious to everyone who is at all concerned about the welfare of Canadian agriculture that the sugar beet growing industry is not a matter to be lightly treated.
The second by-product is beet pulp. Beet pulp is fed to livestock both wet and dry. What is it? It consists of the remains of the beet after the beet has been passed through the factory, sliced and the sugar containing fluid drawn out of the beet. One ton of beets produce 100 pounds of dried beet pulp, according to reference No. 106, 1939, which I referred to a few moments ago as having been presented by the Canada and Dominion sugar factory.
In the last few years men have perfected processes whereby the beet pulp can be dried, shipped far away and preserved indefinitely. This fact is of great importance to our nation in the matter of feed supply in the event that we should, for any reason, have a failure in our forage crops in any given year; and that is something which can easily take place in any part of Canada.
Dried beet pulp is an extremely valuable feed. No other product on the market possesses its virtues. It is both an appetizer and a conditioner. It makes cattle eat more of other feed, digest it better and improve in condition. Milk cows fed with it produce more milk and more milk per pound of feed consumed. Feeder cattle fed with it gain weight faster and add more flesh per pound of feed. Show cattle take on a bloom which cannot be produced as economically in any other way. In 1938 the price was $15.30 f.o.b.
68108-54J
The Address-Mr. Blackmore the factory. This I gather from this reference to which I referred, namely reference No. 106 which will be the name by which I will refer to it from now on.
Beet pulp fresh has succulence of tremendous virtue for stock. Those who have fed milk cows without beet pulp and who have then fed beet pulp for the first time find themselves completely astounded at the results which come from feeding the cows beet pulp. W. N. Hermis, R. E. Miller and R. D. Jones say in Sugar Beet Bulletin, volume 5, 1941, No. 3, paragraphs 61-63: "A ton of silage pulp replaces 139-9 pounds of ground barley, 636 pounds of alfalfa hay, 44 [DOT] 2 pounds of molasses in feeding lambs." This is mentioned in the Alberta sugar beet growers' 1941 report at page 27. Lambs fed on wet pulp made even faster and cheaper gains.
Here is the second by-product of sugar beet. I ask any man in the house or in the country this question: Does he suppose for one minute that the Canadian people and the Canadian government can afford to neglect beet sugar production in this country, judging from the standard of feed alone?
I come now to the third of the by-products, namely beet molasses. What is it? It is what is left after the sugar has been taken out of the beet juice drawn from the beets. There is a certain point beyond which it is not economical to take the sugar out; it costs more to take it out than to leave it in. What is left is called beet molasses. It is a thick, dark substance, in some respects resembling crude molasses with which most hon. members are at least in some degree familiar.
How much beet molasses comes from beets? Four per cent of the beets is the general amount or 80 pounds of beet molasses per ton of beets. This varies to some extent, according to a number of factors, but that is a good general rule. It consists of sucrose to the extent of 50 per cent, soluble salts and water. It is rich in potash and contains some nitrogen. Beet molasses is useful for stock feed, for yeast making, for distilling, and for mixing with dried beet pulp. It is used increasingly in chemical processes, according to Messrs. F. O. Licht in a memorandum prepared for the economic committee of the league of nations in 1929 at page 25. This will be found in reference No. 106 to which I have referred, 1939, at page 25.
Approximately four gallons of alcohol is procured from the molasses of one ton of beets. The average sale price of beet molasses was $20.04 per ton in Alberta, according to E. D. Battrum in the 1943 report, page 12, of the Alberta beet growers' association. Canada
844	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Blackmore and Dominion Sugar Company's submission, reference No. 106, 1939, says of molasses at page 52:
From ten to fifteen thousand tons are produced annually, depending on the yield, test and purity of the beet crop. The total gross value in recent years has averaged over $100,000 annually.
That is from the Ontario factory areas with which most hon. members from Ontario are familiar. So much for the molasses. Judged from the molasses alone from beet sugar production, one would say that, under ordinary circumstances, any nation would be well advised to have the guarantee of an abundance of such molasses being produced domestically every year.
I mentioned beet tailings. What are they? Beet tailings are the little roots on the beets which are broken off when the beets begin to be processed. They are good for feeding swine, sheep and other animals as long as they last, which of course is not long. They are a fairly valuable by-product.
Because of the drying of beet pulp, sugar factories have begun to mix beet molasses along with the beet pulp and dry the two together. This mixture is being found to be an exceedingly valuable feed. I am reading now from an article by T. George Wood who was for years the president of Canadian Sugar Factories Limited in southern Alberta. In an article which appeared in Silver Sunshine in 1950 he says:
Weight and water in wet beet pulp has restricted, its use to those beet farmers within a somewhat close radius of the sugar factories. Only from 10 to 12 per cent of wet beet pulp is actual feed, and hauling costs are high.
He goes on to discuss dried beet pulp as follows:
Dried molasses beet pulp, as produced at the Taber sugar factory, will contain about 25 per cent of molasses dried with the sliced beet residue. It can be used to make up balanced rations of such combination of feeds that will allow every beet farmer to get full livestock production at lower costs. Such a ration should be based largely on home produced feeds.
Dried molasses beet pulp is in all beet districts where it is produced, one of the best and most popular concentrates for feeding to dairy cows, beef cattle and for finishing sheep and lambs.
And again:
Nutritionists stress the need of making concentrate mixtures with sufficient bulk to aid disgestion.
Every farmer knows that in feeding grain alone there is a tendency to form a sticky, pasty mass that becomes indigestible, and is likely to cause bloat and other disgestive troubles causing animals to go off feed.
Now that dried molasses beet pulp becomes available, it should form 25 per cent of the feeding ration throughout all the feeding projects in southern Alberta.
The expanding bulk of dried molasses beet pulp plays a most vital part as a digestive aid because of

its water absorbing quality. It will take up five or six times its original weight in water without producing gas or bloat.
It is easy to feed. Used dry the animal will provide the water. It will make cheap farm feeds palatable and nutritious.
And further:
According to a summary of 42 fattening tests conducted by agricultural experiment stations, each ton of dried beet pulp fed with grain and alfalfa replaced 1782-2 pounds of corn and 835-6 pounds of alfalfa in producing gains on cattle or lambs. This means that each pound of dried pulp saved -89 pounds of grain and -42 pounds of alfalfa, or was approximately equal to 1-15 pounds of grain. The high fattening value of dried pulp is in part due to its ability when mixed with grain to keep fattening animals on feed without any set-backs and thereby to produce steady and uninterrupted gains. As a rule, it is customary to feed dried pulp, if available, as one-quarter to one-half of the grain ration. When used with supplemental feeds, however, such as mill feed, bran, corn-fodder or ensilage, it can be substituted for the entire grain ration if necessary.
I apologize to hon, members for taking so much time to read, but I should like them to know that what I am saying is absolutely authentic and can be relied on one hundred per cent. So much for the pulp and molasses mixture.
How does sugar beet culture affect the soil? Sugar beet culture wisely employed by Germany between 1870 and September 1, 1903, increased that nation's yield of cereals from 14 bushels an acre to 34-9 bushels an acre, which sounds astonishing, does it not? Over that same period Germany paid out $340 million in subsidies, benefiting the beet sugar industry.
Sugar beet culture thereby enabled Germany to support her population in respect of wheat, barley, oats and rye. Germany, in becoming the greatest grower of sugar beets, increased her average yield of cereals 80 per cent over the period 1879 to 1909. Over the period 1919 to 1923 the average yield of wheat in Germany was 26 bushels an acre as against 16-04 bushels an acre for Canada. Messrs. F. O. Licht, the well-known international sugar statisticians, reported these facts to the economic committee of the league of nations in 1929.
How comes this about? Well, in producing sugar beets they use a rotation. This is a rotation which is being worked upon by the Lethbridge experimental farm: Thirty tons per acre of manure are scattered upon the land upon which it is intended to raise beets. Then beets are raised for two years; then wheat is raised one year; then alfalfa is raised for three years; then wheat for one year, and then 30 tons of manure are put on again. Now, in order to get the best results with sugar beets some such rotation has to

be used. Consequently the result is an encouraging improvement of the soil.
Here is a vegetable, through the growing of which, Canadian farmers in certain regions can produce for Canadians two highly valuable crops at the same time, sugar, an indispensable human food, and sugar beet byproducts, which, taken together, constitute perhaps the finest stock feed known to man. Surely the considered conclusion of all informed and enlightened Canadians must be that the sugar beet growing industry must be recognized, respected and then treated, as a branch of Canadian agriculture, second to none, the peer of all, worthy to be the queen of all.
What must be the estimate of any Canadian government that would permit the agricultural business of beet growing to be seriously injured?

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to have this opportunity to say a few words at this time. First of all, I am sure I cannot add to the many kind expressions that have been conveyed to the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. At the same time I should like to convey to them my personal congratulations on the very fine addresses they gave at the opening of this session of parliament.
Since I represent a British Columbia constituency I want to say to our own Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) how much we appreciate the fact that two outstanding members of our province have been elevated to high and honoured positions in the cabinet. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) does not come here as a man inexperienced in that industry. Fifty per cent of his constituency is bordered by the fishing industry. He has always been closely connected with it, and as an engineer by profession I am sure he will make an outstanding and successful job of his position as Minister of Fisheries in the federal government. The Solicitor General (Mr. Campney) is certainly well qualified to hold the position he occupies in the Department of Justice, since he is a member of one of the largest legal firms in the west. Because of that I am sure he comes here with considerable knowledge to fulfil that position. He is also Associate Minister of National Defence. I might say that he is one of many of us who had to do the tough job of marching as private soldiers in the first world war. Later on he was promoted to the ranks of the flying corps as a flying officer. I am sure his outstanding
The Address-Mr. Mott knowledge as a veteran fits him well for the position of Associate Minister of National Defence.
At this time, Mr. Speaker, I also wish to convey my thanks to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and his colleagues in the cabinet for their assistance and help last year in the development of the harbour and port of New Westminster. The loan of $1,250,000 to the harbour board for the extension and expansion of our docks, that we need in the west so urgently at this time, will go a long way toward taking care of the extensions that we can foresee before many years. I should like to express sincere appreciation to the citizens for the fact that only a few days ago they passed a bylaw in which they turned waterfront property valued at about $100,000 over to the crown for the sum of one dollar. That bylaw was passed by a majority of four to one. It shows the deep appreciation of the people of New Westminster.
Then there are some other matters I should like to discuss at this time, matters which have been brought to my attention in my own constituency, and which I think it is only proper that I place on record. The first of these has to do with the returned veterans. I do not refer to all of them, but more particularly to the burnt-out pensioners to whom the war veterans allowance would apply.
A few days ago I listened to the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) when he spoke concerning the veterans. I noted that during his observations he made use of an old saying we always associate with the late R. L. Borden. I think many of us will remember those words all too well. They were brief. His statement was that nothing would be too good for the veterans of the war when they returned. I may not be using his exact words, but I believe my recollection of them gives the proper meaning.
Let me say here that, along with many thousands of others, I returned from the first war. We might very easily place emphasis on the word "nothing" in that saying. Each of us received $70 a month for six months if we had served three years in the Canadian expeditionary force. We received $35 for a suit of clothes-and while clothing might not have been as expensive as it is today, it was certainly more expensive than it was at the time those young fellows entered the army. That $70 a month was given (to us while we were looking for employment, and we know that in that same year there were some 55,000 returned soldiers from the first war who went to the United

The Address-Mr. Mott States looking for employment. At that time there was no organization such as the Canadian Legion to look after the veterans who returned from the war. That is why I now mention that in my view it is necessary that some further assistance be given to them.
I am not going to quote what the hon. member for Battle River said, because it is all to be found at ipage 314 of Hansard for December 3 and hon. members may look it up if they wish. I would point out, however, that he quoted the remarks made in 1931 by the late Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, in which he set out the plan he had at that time for the veterans of the first war. It showed progressive thinking, and anyone wishing to read it will understand it as well as I do. It shows that not only the late Mr. Mackenzie King but other governments since that time have been acting progressively in trying to assist the veterans. It is true those veterans have not received everything for which they have asked, and this, of course, is no indication that they are not entitled to what they have asked. In this connection my mind goes back to the veterans affairs committee, of which I was a member, and the efforts of the opposition to embarrass the government by pointing out that everything that had been requested had not been given. I believe the disabled veterans received more than they asked for. Then there have been many other grants to widows and also for the educational advancement of orphans. I do feel, however, that the burnt-out pensioner has not received, to the full extent, what he should have had.
I am not going to follow the example of my hon. friends opposite by saying that we should give them this and give them that and then, in the next breath, preach economy and ask the government to cut down personal and corporation income tax. I am not going to ask that, while at the same time asking for large amounts for social services. I agree to a certain extent with our friends in the C.C.F. party when they ask for increased social services. I do not know whether I have heard them ask that the income tax be cut, but I do know the party sitting to the right of them, from where I stand, in company with the official opposition, seem to be preaching a program of economy at this time.
I have noticed that other hon. members who have discussed veterans' problems have not made the fiery speeches they have made on so many occasions. They have not placed themselves on record with such high pressure as they have formerly. Some have said that if a committee on veterans' affairs is .appointed they would like to serve on it, but


I have noticed that they have quietened down considerably in their pressure on behalf of the veterans, if one compares what they have said recently with what they have said in the past.
While I stand in my place and ask the government to assist these veterans, and go along with hon. members of the opposition and on this side of the house in stating that it is necessary to give further assistance to burnt-out pensioners, I cannot in the same breath ask the government to cut down on personal and corporation taxation. I am not one who believes that on the one hand you can ask for heavier expenditures by the government and, on the other, expect lower taxation.
This is all I am going to say, except that I hope the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) will take note of what I have said. I realize, of course, that even this small request would cost two or three million dollars. The war veterans assistance fund, which was taken away last year for two months after the increase in the war veterans allowance, has not worked out very satisfactorily, but it is my hope that even today the allowance will be of great assistance to them, and I would hope that something further will be done to restore it.
I should like to say a few words about our situation on the lower mainland in British Columbia, in connection with television. I come from a constituency located twelve miles from Vancouver, known as the hub of the Fraser valley-and I am sorry the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) is not in his seat, because I know he would have some comment to make. For many years, however, my constituency has been so described. There are some 150,000 people in the area, including one who has the funds and the equipment to instal television. I have no quarrel with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as I think they have done a wonderful job in providing service in places where private stations would not have spread out if it had been left to private enterprise to handle our radio in the past. I think the same about television. We need cultural and other types of programs which they will broadcast. We are going to require that type of program. We now get certain television programs from the United States. I have a television set and I get good programs from Seattle, 145 miles away, the type of television program that the ordinary person wants to see. I have been connected with sports nearly all my life, and when I am home on a Friday night I like to see four or five good boxing matches from Madison Square Garden or Detroit. I have seen practically every big football game which has been played in

the United States. We receive many good sports programs, besides plays and other things of interest which we enjoy.
My main reason for bringing up this matter is what is happening in Bellingham, a city of some 35,000 people about 19 miles from the border and about 40 miles from New Westminster. A television station is being installed in that city. The following article appeared in a New Westminster newspaper. It is a B.U.P. dispatch from Victoria and reads:
Plans of Bellingham radio station operator Roger Jones to set up a television station serving both Washington and British Columbia will be proceeded with immediately, it was learned today in Victoria.
David M. Armstrong, manager of Victoria radio station CKDA, said he learned from Jones that the Bellingham television outlet is expected to be approved within a few months, and will not be delayed three years, as first reported.
Jones, operator of radio station KVOS, confirmed that he planned to beam programs to British Columbia, using B.C. talent, and said he will accept advertising from B.C. firms.
Armstrong conferred with Jones today in Bellingham, discussing technical problems in establishing television outlets. The Victoria radio station manager plans to set up a TV outlet in the capital city as soon as his application is approved by the C.B.C.
I hope the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) will take notice of that. Here is a station being set up in a city only 20 miles from the Canadian border with the avowed intention of coming into Canada to get advertising and beaming programs to Canada from the United States. I know it is the intention of the government to put television in Vancouver, but I submit that where there is need for a station the government should fix a certain time limit for private industry to indicate whether they wish to set up a station. That is all I am going to say about television at this time.
I do want to say a few words with regard to this great discussion that has taken place during the last few days regarding the Currie report. I want to reply to some of the points brought out in the criticism by the official opposition and other parties. First I want to make it clear that my army experience was as a private soldier. As you all know, that is the lowest rank you can have; there is no one under you. I see the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra (Mr. Green) smiling. I am not ashamed to say that I served three years and two months in the Canadian expeditionary force and came out a private soldier. I must have been a good private to remain in that position three years and two months. Nevertheless I did gain some experience of the Canadian army.
Reference has been made to pilfering, but I think the only pilfering I did was to take
The Address-Mr. Mott the $1.10 per day they gave me for three years. Some of the things in this report amused me and some of the points raised by the opposition also amused me. I think one of the main things on which you should have put your finger has been left out absolutely. The other day when this matter first came up for consideration it reminded me of a real military operation somewhere, with all the lieutenant colonels that were taking part. I have nothing against lieutenant colonels or generals. All these lieutenant colonels and other marched in just as they used to years ago; they had their operation orders under their- arms, but instead of using heavy artillery, all they had was pop guns and firecrackers.
One thing was quite noticeable. In this report which had taken that length of time to prepare and which covered so many matters, you had to jump one, two, three and four pages to find one line to complain about.
What a line.

It was quite noticeable that you stayed down at the bottom with some of the things, where some of this trouble started, and then went to the top to hit the administration. Why did you hit the administration? You hit the administration because you wanted to get at the minister. The only way you could get at him was to attack the administration.
An order was sent out by the deputy minister to the quartermaster general. Did any of the lieutenant colonels on that side repeat that? I never heard one of them refer to it. They know enough about organization and military matters, and I know enough about them as a private, to know that 90 per cent of the troubles refer to discipline. It does not come from the Minister of National Defence; it is discipline.
All those who are returned soldiers know that when we were over in England and wanted an extra bucket of coal in the night, we formed our own little operation. We went up to the guard at the fence and two of us kept him engaged there while two more crawled over the fence to get the coal. That is part of army life, and everyone knows that.
Those who were in the army of occupation after the war know that these things happened. How many of those officers across from us in the official opposition who were speaking on this question walked down the streets of cities in the Ruhr, in Brussels and other places and saw girl after girl and young lady after young lady walking by in beautiful coats made out of our blankets. They never had such clothes. These things occur in the army to a certain extent and the only way

The Address-Mr. Mott to stop them is through discipline, not by trying to get at the administration or the Minister of National Defence.
I notice some other things. Reference has been made to a hobby horse or something else. Today with our mechanized army we really have an army of tradesmen. If you are up in Churchill, not at Petawawa, gracious sakes alive; if someone wanted to build something, should that be investigated in this manner? These things can be enlarged upon, it can be said they are made out of mahogany or gold or something else, but it is much better for soldiers or officers to be busy making these things in their spare time. If they have nothing else to do in their spare time I think they should be encouraged to follow a hobby and make these things. It may not be horses but something else. Take the air force in the last war. Look at the number of A-l mechanics who came out of it. Some of them were overenergetic, and while they were studying and learning their trades they made many small things that they brought out of the service with them as souvenirs. I do not think we should be too critical of these things.
I get a laugh out of the horses. In the war in which I served horses were used for transportation. Horses or our feet; that was all we had. In our mechanized army of today I wonder if we have requisitions with "horse" marked on them. In looking over the requisitions to find one marked "horse" probably they could not find one, so the cost was charged to labour. It is labour just the same as the labour of man. The horse is a living animal just as man is a living person, and probably that is why it was charged to labour, although that may not be the case. We should look into these problems to find out whether or not the criticism that has been levelled is correct.
As one who served under the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) when he was general officer commanding the reserve army on the Pacific coast in the last war, I should like to ask him in a friendly spirit-he does not need to reply but I know he will agree with me-if many thousands of courts of inquiries were not reported to him concerning things that were lost. We all know what happened when a pair of binoculars or a revolver was lost. If you were the officer commanding a small unit with the rank of captain you got $240 a year and were charged with looking after $80,000 worth of equipment. They gave you two sergeants, a quartermaster sergeant and an orderly room sergeant and expected you, on a salary of $240 a year, to be responsible for $80,000 worth of equipment. I can prove that because I was

in that position. If you lost something you did not have much to pay for it out of $240 a year when you had to provide your army equipment, buy a suit of clothes and other small things and keep up with the Joneses. What did you do? In your own mind you probably knew that a certain article was gone, so you sent to brigade headquarters and they set up a court of inquiry. You could call the article lost or stolen, but it was gone. It did not always fall through the floor.
I know there have probably been thousands of such courts of inquiry. A lot of these things go with the army and always will. There is no doubt about that. Today in Canada it is difficult to get men to serve in the permanent forces. Men were quite willing to do so when they could go overseas and get into action, for the adventure or otherwise, but they are not so willing to serve in the permanent forces. Therefore I wonder how serious some of these things are from the point of view of the veteran. I think when the facts become well known to the thousands of private soldiers and other ranks of the first war and to the thousands who served in the last war they will realize that they ran into the same thing during their army life. I do not say they should steal railway tracks, but at the same time I was amused by that incident. I will be fair with the opposition. I do not condone the removal of two Canadian Pacific railway tracks and their replacement by tracks taken from the Canadian National but it is a strange thing that the railway companies did not notice what was taking place.
In any event I will be interested in hearing the remarks that are still to be made, but as a private soldier I want to assure the opposition that they certainly have not convinced me that this matter is as serious as their speeches would indicate. In the first place we had already heard about the Petawawa scandal on the floor of the house. Now we are opening up the matter again, which is only the right and proper thing to do; but I do not think the matter is going to turn out to be as serious as the opposition are trying to make it appear.
I am very glad to have had the opportunity of saying a few words. I am leaving tomorrow morning, and I appreciate the opportunity of being allowed to speak at this time. Three years ago I said a few words in the house and this is only my second attempt. I am not going to take up any more time, because I am certain there are many others who wish to speak before we adjourn for the Christmas holidays.

Mr. J. A, Richard (Si. Maurice-Lafleche):
Mr. Speaker, it is with deep emotion and a sense of profound national pride that I address the house. May I first be permitted to offer my sincere congratulations and thanks to the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne; they have both fulfilled their task in an admirable way.
Without going into every detail, I must say that the speech from the throne delivered at the beginning of this session of the twenty-first parliament mentions projects of the highest importance for the economic development and general welfare of the country at large. I am confident that all members of the house, including those of the opposition, are greatly desirous- of fulfilling their important duty as representatives of their compatriots, conscientiously and without ever losing sight of the common good and general interest of the people.
From the house I wish to send my best regards to the people of St. Maurice-Lafleche, whom I have the honour and privilege of representing, and I wish to thank them sincerely for the confidence they have placed in me.
It gives me great pleasure to associate myself with the other members of the house who have tendered their congratulations to His Eminence Cardihal Leger, Archbishop of Montreal, who has been raised to the rank of cardinal of the Roman Catholic church. I do so on behalf of all those of the same faith and in particular in the name of the good people of the constituency of St. Maurice-Lafleche. His Eminence may be assured of our admiration, deep respect and filial devotion.
I also congratulate our Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, whose talents are recognized all over the commonwealth and have brought him his new title of doctor of the university of London. Our whole country is, undoubtedly, very proud of her brilliant Prime Minister.
There is another member of this house who, since he has been in public life, has spared neither his time nor his experience in the administration of the department entrusted to him and whose task is probably one of the most delicate and difficult. I refer to the Hon. the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) who was recently honoured with a doctor's degree from Laval university. I beg the hon. minister to accept my most sincere compliments and congratulations.	1
The Address-Mr. J. A. Richard
In awarding this doctorate to such an outstanding person, Laval university has given recognition to one of the best promoters of national unity. For this we must give thanks to the broad-mindedness of the Secretary of State for External Affairs with regard to French language and culture in this country. All my fellow Quebeckers are, I am sure, happy at what Laval university has just done.
Mr. Speaker, I turn now to another subject.
I wish to acquaint you better with the St. Maurice district and particularly with the constituency of St. Maurice-Lafleche which I represent here. I will attempt to make these remarks as brief as possible, after which I will submit my suggestions for the industrial, agricultural and touristic advancement of this lovely part of my province.
My constituency has three main industrial towns, all situated on the banks of the St. Maurice river, whose total population now exceeds sixty thousand. First we have the town of Shawinigan, where I live, and whose population is now up to the thirty thousand mark, exclusive of the suburban community of Almaville or Shawinigan South, known as the largest village in Canada, with a population of ten thousand in itself. The town of Shawinigan is twenty miles north of Three Rivers. Although only fifty-one years old, she is the princess city of Mauricia. Her people hope that, before long, she will become the queen of Mauricia, with all due deference to my worthy colleague, the member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer). You will find in our city a peaceful population, hard-working citizens and a competent labouring class. In addition to the electric power plants of the Shawinigan Water and Power, we have pulp and paper mills, aluminum carbide, textile and electro-chemical products plants of great importance. In addition to those already mentioned, there are about twenty industries of secondary importance which provide work for the people.
The city of Grand Mere is today separated from Shawinigan, so to speak, only by an imaginary line, since owing to the progress and expansion of these two sister cities, houses have multiplied along the whole distance between these two industrial centres. The population of Grand Mere is about 13,000. Its main industries are paper, textile and shoemaking.
If one travels northward for about sixty miles, along the St. Maurice, one comes to the nice little city of La Tuque, which has a population of 12,000; these people derive their living from an important pulp mill and numerous other private enterprises. In the neighbourhood of these three cities I have

The Address-Mr. J. A. Richard just mentioned, there are twenty-seven rural parishes. We may say, therefore, that the farmers of this area have ready markets which, in spite of the difficulties inherent to the area, are very useful to them.
I should like also to point out that the St. Maurice valley with its large fields, beautiful mountains, game-abounding forests and well-stocked lakes is admired and enjoyed by all nature-loving people. The tourist who pays a visit to this district cannot but be wonder-struck, cannot but prolong his stay and come back to it. This area offers all facilities for industrial development, so much so that, at a congress of professional engineers held recently at Shawinigan, a famous engineer stated that the St. Maurice area has known such an industrial expansion for the last fifty years that it deserves to be called the industrial valley of Canada.
Is this not an eloquent testimony to the participation of our district in Canadian industry? Hydroelectric power has always been the main factor in this rapid development; it is responsible for all our industrial production in its various forms. As a matter of fact there are seven power plants set up over a 125 mile stretch of the St. Maurice river, with a total capacity of approximately 206,000,000 horsepower. The total value of industrial production in the town of Shawinigan alone exceeds $90 million. The towns of Grand Mere and La Tuque also have industries with an annual production figure of several million dollars.
Our standing orders prevent me from reading into the record the names of any of the industrial concerns of a particular district. Nevertheless I would invite anybody who is interested to come and visit them on the spot.
I therefore suggest to the government the possibility of further developing Canadian industry with due regard to all the advantages offered by the St. Maurice district. According to Mr. G. K. Sheils, president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, industrialists will, in the next few months, invest one billion dollars in- plant construction and equipment.
As for the tourist trade, which always brings in considerable returns, I suggest we come to some agreement with our neighbours, concerning the stabilization at parity level of both currencies. Either side would thus succeed in avoiding numerous annoyances and such an agreement would further profit the tourist trade.
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of numerous heads of families in my county may I address the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott)? I should


like to voice their complaints about the income tax scale. They have asked for exemptions up to $3,000. Considering the very high cost of -living and the numerous obligations of those who have a wife and children, I feel convinced that all the complaints I have received are absolutely sincere.
I agree that a tax reduction in this category of wage earners would entail a notable reduction in public revenue. However, considering the normal increase in the budget for each fiscal year, would it not be -possible to find compensation for this loss of revenue, while granting relief to the small wage earners?
It is no secret that there is in the province of Quebec a political movement known as the "Union des Electeurs". Like most hon. members, I believe, I receive numerous protests, resolutions and requests for amendment regarding some of our social and economic legislation. I have no doubt about the complete sincerity of those people. This at least tends to show the deep interest they are taking in all that pertains to public business, and I congratulate them for it. Some of their requests are fair and deserve to be taken into -consideration by the government. However, for the time being, it is impossible under our constitution to implement some of the reforms advocated by the "Union des Electeurs". These gentlemen may rest assured that I am always willing to receive their constructive suggestions and help them whenever possible.
In regard to the thorny problem of taxation agreements between the province of Quebec and the central government, there is little I could add to the recent and quite appropriate speech made by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix) and the comments of the member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier). However, I ask all members of the house to take the trouble of examining the facts, not from the point of view of selfinterest, but carefully and objectively.
I might add that it would be much easier to come to an agreement if the Quebec government did not make a political issue out of the matter. In spite of what our opponents may think, the central government has always been very generous towards the provinces, although it does not seek all the credit for it. Too many people are completely in the dark about the large contribution made by the federal government to the cost of old age pensions and family allowances, which in my constituency amount to $2,804,000 per year. In addition, there are grants to universities, to hospitals and other national contributions to all kinds of associations devoted to the improvement of health services, to mention but those.

The Address-Mr. Knowles
To come back to this business of publicity,
I wonder how we must take the audacity of a certain Union Nationale member who, merely for reasons of publicity, no doubt, had his picture printed in a daily newspaper, handing over a cheque for $100,000 to the mother superior of a religious congregation in a great fit of generosity. Now this happens to be a federal grant. I was anxious to put matters right for the information of several people who have been misled and in order to warn the people against this type of political propaganda indulged in by our opponents.
I now come to another matter which has been mentioned very often in previous debates, that is, the question of a national flag. It will undoubtedly be said that the matter is under consideration, that a committee has already been formed to investigate the matter and so on and so forth, but the fact remains that Canada is still without a national flag.
Don't you find it rather strange, Mr. Speaker, that a free country like ours, both great and rich, a country that ranks among the great nations of the world, has been so long without a truly distinctive national flag?
In 1950, I had the great privilege of making a pilgrimage to Rome. Before leaving Europe, I made it a point to stay a few weeks in France, Belgium and Holland in order to visit the most important historical sites. Among these, Dieppe and Vimy, where so many Canadians won distinction for their bravery during the first great war, drew my attention and that of my three companions, Commander Albert Giguere, Rev. Raymond Cossette, parish priest, and Mr. Harry Desaulniers, a Shawinigan merchant. Accompanied by a French guide, who was a very eloquent patriot, I had the opportunity of examining at Vimy the tremendous work done by our soldiers as a prelude to a glorious victory. I read many of the names inscribed on the base of the huge monument. Many of these names were well known to us. These soldiers gave their lives to safeguard our liberties. My feelings of respect, pride and gratitude towards these courageous men were somewhat mixed with a certain feeling of uneasiness, which I could not hide. I would have liked to see these graves decorated with a national flag. Let us hope that before long those who thus gave their lives will receive from their country this last tribute. Their sublime sacrifice is worth it.
As we are now in the Christmas season, I take this opportunity to offer to this house my best wishes. My greetings go first to the Right Hon. the Prime Minister and to every member of his cabinet. I wish health,
happiness and a long life to these men who contribute so much to the progress and development of our country. I make the same wishes for all members of the Liberal party. I hope that Providence will keep them for a long time to come in their present places.
I would also like to offer my best wishes to the members of the press gallery who spare neither time nor effort to keep the public informed on all social and political events which concern them. Health, happiness and long life; may the work they take on be more and more appreciated all the time.
I would not want to forget the hon. gentlemen who sit on the left. I extend my best wishes to them. May Providence grant them and their families a great deal of happiness, along with good health, and may Canadians continue to have only limited confidence in their administrative capacity, for the greatest good of the great majority of the citizens of this country.
