speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) indicated that the Acting Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) would be speaking some time today with reference to the Currie report. I think it is fair to say that most hon. members of the house have been waiting with some anticipation for that speech. I too have been waiting for it for several hours. But since he is still in his place and has not yet chosen to speak, I feel that I should say a few words by way of comment on what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) had to say this morning.
At the outset I want to congratulate the Prime Minister for his forthrightness in the statement he made concerning the fact that there had been an earlier draft of the Currie report in which changes had been made before it was presented to this house, in confirmation of the evidence which I presented on Monday. As I say, I congratulate him on his forthrightness in taking the house into his confidence, as he did; although, along with many other members in this house, I was shocked by what he was called upon to reveal.
He has confirmed the fact that before this report was presented to the house an earlier copy was placed in the hands of the deputy minister of the department that was being investigated, and that that deputy minister apparently was given the opportunity to "vet" the report before it was put in its final form.

The Address-Mr. Knowles I congratulate the Prime Minister for his directness in replying to one of my questions when he said that he himself was a bit surprised that this course had been pursued. I think the surprise he felt was felt even more strongly by many of us in this house.
Here is a case of a department being investigated as a result of certain scandalous events that took place. That investigation arose out of a demand in this house that such an inquiry be made. The promise that the investigation would be made, that it would be thorough and that it would be objective was given to this house by the responsible minister. As we now know, the report is a serious indictment of at least certain sections of that department and the people who come under that minister. Yet it appears that before it was put in its final form, the top people in that department were given a chance to look at the indictment that was to be made of them and to suggest certain changes. Mr. Speaker, most of us in this house feel that is a scandalous way in which to carry out an investigation of this kind. I confess that I felt a bit sorry for the Prime Minister in that he had to admit to the house that this had been done.
I wish also to extend my congratulations to the Prime Minister for something else. I do it with respect to the restraint which I felt he exercised in relation to another aspect of this whole matter. I can imagine some individuals in public life trying to cover up the really serious aspect of the matter by dragging in any red herring that might be found. I can imagine some persons in political life trying to blow up the questions which he asked of me. But he merely asked-and let it go at that-as to how the earlier copy of this report came into the possession of my leader the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). He asked the question-[DOT] which was one of natural interest; I find a similar interest all over this building-as to how that copy of the report came into the possession of my leader; but he asked it and let it go at that. In other words, he recognized the fact-and he made that clear to the house in what he said this morning-that the important aspect of the matter with which I confronted him on Monday, arising out of the fact that we had in our possession this earlier copy, was the question as to how the changes came to be made and why they were made.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that I have been in touch with my leader by telephone since this morning's sitting. I regret that, owing to illness, he is not able to be with us this week. He expressed to me the same view as that which I took from the Prime Minister's

statement this morning, namely that the important question is not how he came into possession of the earlier copy but rather as to how and why the changes came to be made. In the light of that fact, I say on behalf of my leader that he does not feel obligated to say anything further at this time as to how this report came into his possession. He feels that the important thing for him to do has been done, namely that use should be made of the information that was in his possession so the public might find out what had happened. It is now clear to everyone that if he had not done so-if he had not carried out that obligation by asking me to raise this matter in the house on Monday-we would never have known that this report, this indictment of the Department of National Defence, was placed in the hands of the deputy minister for him to "vet" before it was presented in its final form to the minister and, through him, to the house.
As I have already said, we regard this as a very shocking situation. To us it indicates the attitude that seems to prevail in the Department of National Defence. It has already been made clear in the Currie report itself that it is an attitude toward public expenditure which is scandalous; it is an attitude toward public property which is shocking to the Canadian people, but in addition to that there seems to be this feeling on the part of the Department of National Defence that it is top dog, and that nobody has the right to question its decisions or its wisdom, the way it spends money or the way it operates its affairs. When, an investigation is made, it takes the view that that investigation must be submitted to that department and to its top officials before the results of the investigation are made known to the house and to the country.
I was similarly astounded on Monday- and I feel even more that way when I go over the records in connection, with this matter-at the fact that the Prime Minister when he tabled the report on Monday, gave us at the same time a memorandum on the Currie report signed by the chief of the general staff. I shall have something to say in a few moments about one of the paragraphs in that memorandum, but what I am saying at the moment is that there seems to be this attitude in the Department of National Defence. To me it is so at the political level, with the minister, and it seems to be so at the general staff level as well, that somehow or other they feel they are top dogs, that they can run the show in whatever way they say. That attitude is clear from what the Prime Minister said in answer to a question which

my deskmate, the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) asked yesterday when he inquired as to why that memorandum from the chief of the general staff was presented along with the report. "Why, simply because the chief of the general staff asked that it be done." That was, in effect, the Prime Minister's answer. Well, who is running this government? Who is to decide what is to be laid before the house when an investigation is being made into this department? I thought it was understood that Mr. Currie was making the investigation, and that all we asked for, all we were to be given, was his report. But, said the Prime Minister yesterday, at pages 764 and 765 of Hansard, in the midst of the speech of my deskmate:
The explanation was that General Simonds requested that it be done.
It reminds me, Mr. Speaker, of an incident back in the days when Your Honour first assumed the chair as Speaker of this house.
I refer to the flour milling report. You remember the information that we got at that time. It appears that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) showed that report to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). He did not like the looks of it. So he said to the Minister of Justice that that report must not be made public unless there was another statement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce at the same time so that the report of Mr. McGregor would not be misunderstood. Well, we took a very serious view of that position then. I take the same view now with respect to the apparent insistence by the chief of the general staff that at the very moment the Currie report was tabled, indicting the Department of National Defence, there had to be at the same time' a memorandum from the chief of the general staff making certain explanations and demanding that Mr. Currie substantiate some of the statements that were made in that document. Well, Mr. Speaker, I ask you the question: Who is running the show around here, anyway? This is a democracy. The elected people are the ones who should be in charge, and I do not think the chief of the general staff even had the right to make a request like that to the Prime Minister, let alone the Prime Minister yielding to that request.
I have had something to say about the memorandum by General Simonds. I note in particular that the part of Mr. Currie's report that he dislikes the most is referred to in paragraph 6 of his memorandum. The reference is to a certain section in the first part of the report, which brings us directly
The Address-Mr. Knowles to the notorious page 17. As I say, I appreciated the forthrightness with which the Prime Minister spoke this morning when he admitted, in reply to questions that were put to him later, that there were some questions to which he did not know the answers, and he said he would try and ascertain the answers in due course.
I think we have to be told somewhere along the line the full story about page 17 of the Currie report. The Prime Minister said this morning that he was informed that it was not the subject of discussion on December 1, at any rate, between Mr. Drury, the deputy minister, and the representatives of Mr. Currie. Later on in the same discussion this morning the Prime Minister said he had no explanation to offer for the changes on page 17. We find in the memorandum of the chief of the general staff that there is a particular complaint about page 17. We now know that the report, before it appeared in its final form, was in the hands of the deputy minister of national defence. We do not know yet whether he showed it _ to others. One of the questions I should like to ask is whether that copy of the original draft, which apparently has been returned to Mr. Currie, has on it the initials of other people who saw it, and if so how many people did initial it? At any rate, it is clear that it was in the department, that they had a look at it, and for reasons that have not been given, not been explained, it turns out that on page 17, which directs certain remarks against those at or near the top, certain changes have been made. As a matter of fact there were two changes on that page. One of them is already well known, the original having read:
But, if this spirit permeated the lower echelons of the army, it is more difficult to condone the same attitudes at or near the top.
As everybody knows, this was changed to read:
-it is more difficult to condone the same attitudes higher up.
In addition to that there was a slight change in the rest of the wording of that page. It goes on to read in the original form:
There, a higher degree both of intelligence and responsibility is essential. It was not present in the degree required.
The version laid on the table of the house by the Prime Minister has the word "always" inserted, so that it reads:
It was not always present in the degree required.
Now, the interesting point about the changes on that page is that they seem to soften the indictment on that page and in particular they seem to withdraw a bit of the heat that was directed toward some of those
854	HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Knowles
at or near the top in the army and in the Department of National Defence.
I notice that during the course of this debate there is a tendency on the part of our friends in the official opposition to put all the blame at the political level, and I do not particularly quarrel with them; and I ask them not to get too excited for a moment because I agree with them that in our responsible form of government the final responsibility does rest with the ministers, with the elected people. But they, by putting the full blame there, are eliciting from backbench Liberals around the house interjections that suggest that backbench Liberals think the blame should be put on the general staff. What I do not like about that interchange and that conflict between the Progressive Conservatives and the Liberals is the "either or" aspect of it. It seems to me from the terms of Mr. Currie's report that blame has to be attached at both levels. Blame has to be attached to some of those at the very top in the army itself for permitting condi-T tions which allowed these thefts and this pilfering to take place, and certainly responsibility for there being people at these top levels who would permit that kind of situation rests with the minister himself, and there is no doubt about it that the final responsibility is there. But I think we should make it clear that there is some blame attaching to some of the top army people as well.
Last night the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), who I presume has read the report- although I wondered a bit, from some of the things he said-asserted that in his view the whole difficulty was not to be found in any fault in the auditing system, or other arrangements in vogue in the Department of National Defence, but rather in human frailty. Well, you do not have to read very far in Mr. Currie's report to discover that in his view the case is the very reverse. He tells us that there was an open door, and that the only reason there was not more of this was due to the honesty of so many of the great mass of those in the armed forces. I think this emphasis that the Minister of Justice placed last night on human frailty in reference to members of the armed services was unfair, because Mr. Currie says-and it is right there in the early part of the report-that it was a loose situation, an open door, and the only reason there was not more of this kind of thing was that the men in the armed services had not walked through the door that was left open for them.
Well, the whole situation certainly adds up to a shocking and disgraceful picture, and I hope there will be drastic action to deal with it. There are cries among some of the backbenchers on the Liberal side that something

should be done to some of those on the general staff. Well, anyone in the army itself who is responsible for any of the machinery, the attitudes and the psychology-and particularly that psychology described at page 17-should be dealt with severely. But certainly at the same time, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that a minister who has permitted this sort of thing to go on-and it has been drawn to his attention time and again; it is several years since some of us first referred to some minor things that the auditor general in his report drew to the attention of the Department of National Defence-a minister in whose department there is a state of affairs such as that outlined in the Currie report should be doing something else than being a minister of national defence. And I earnestly hope, even before we can get around to a chance to let the people of Canada decide upon this matter at an election, that the rumours are true that there is going to be a change, and that somebody else will be in charge of this Department of National Defence, important as it is to the people of Canada and spending, as it does, so large a proportion of the public funds of this country.
I must confess I was startled by the lighthearted and nonchalant references made a moment ago by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mott). His references were made to the sort of thing that happens under conditions of actual warfare. Surely that does not justify this kind of thing happening here in Canada in peacetime. I believe that upon reflection the hon. member will regret what he said today, making light as he did of these rather huge transactions in pilfering and in downright thieving. I do not believe the hon. member for New Westminster expressed views that he will stand by. I certainly think they are not the views of Liberal members generally, let alone the rest of us. I think, rather, that all of us take this whole question as one of very serious import and serious consequence, and I hope there will be action at an early date.
With regard to this whole question of changes that were made in the report, I say again that I congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) upon the forthrightness with which he dealt with this question this morning. The fact that these changes were made indicates two things to me. One is that the changes that were made, particularly on page 17, seem to be with an eye to drawing away such heat as can be drawn away from highly placed persons. I do not like that. If highly placed persons are responsible for these conditions, then the report should have said so, as it did in the earlier version.
The other thing I do not like, and that these changes suggest to me, is something to which

I have already referred, namely the attitude the Department of National Defence seems to have, that it is running the show, that even when its administration has been called into question and is being investigated it has the right to see the report on that investigation, in its earlier form, before it is finally presented to the minister for presentation to the house.
I shall say no more at this time. But I do regard, as do all the members of this group, this whole affair as one that is extremely serious.
Is the house ready for the question?

Mr. Speaker, it is very surprising that the members of the government should have been sitting back for three days now, without having a statement of government policy with regard to this Currie report made by one of the ministers. It is even more surprising that this afternoon we should have had the Acting Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) sitting in the house for two hours or more, apparently ready to speak; and yet he has let Your Honour call for the vote on the subamendment, without rising in his place and making any attempt to justify or to clear up this question on behalf of the government. It is also worthy of comment that apparently the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has seen fit to give the junior member of the cabinet the responsibility of explaining the government's stand on this question.
In my 17 years as a member of the house there has not been a more serious or a more damaging report than this Currie report brought before the House of Commons. I am afraid members of the government, and its supporters in the house, do not realize just how serious the report is for the Canadian people. For it is highly critical, highly damaging, even after changes have been made which have the effect of reducing criticism of the government. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has just pointed out, it is so significant that this morning the Prime Minister was unable to explain the most damaging change, that which deleted from the original report the words "at or near the top" and substituted therefor the words "higher up". At the same time the word "always" was inserted, thereby greatly weakening the sentence which was so condemnatory of the Department of National Defence. This insertion makes the sentence now read, "It was not always present in the degree required", whereas the original report contained the sentence, "It was not present in the degree required."
The Address-Mr. Green
This situation is even more serious because the efficiency of the Department of National Defence is most vital at this present time. We are in a period of world tension with the civilized nations of the world divided into two camps, both rearming. We are faced with what is known as a cold war. Canada for the first time is in the position where her shores, and in fact many of her cities and probably most of the key centres, would be under attack in the event of a third world war. We lie on the air route between the Soviet union and the United States, and if a third war should occur Canada would be another Belgium.
This world situation is not one that will end in a matter of weeks or months. It is generally accepted that this period of tension, this cold war, may continue for ten or fifteen or twenty years. Perhaps no one who is in this chamber today will live to see the end of the cold war. As things stand at the present time there will be an end to it only if we go into what will be a very hot war. I repeat that under those conditions the efficiency of the Department of National Defence is vital to the nation.
The efficiency of that department is vital for another reason. Our people are being called upon to make a great effort, essentially in support of this defence department. Our young men are being asked to volunteer for service in Korea and Europe. Many of them have been killed and several hundred others have been wounded. This call is going out to the young men of Canada to make a sacrifice for their country. We see these advertisements in the papers every week urging our young men to enlist, to do their part to help the country. Surely the one thing to which they are entitled, without any question, is to have behind them a Department of National Defence which is even more efficient than any other department of government. It is not a question of the staff, or the minister, or his assistant; the Department of National Defence as a whole should be the most efficient department of government in Canada today.
Not only are young Canadians being called upon for these sacrifices; all Canadians are being taxed to a crippling degree in order to support the work of this defence department. I was amazed to read in the press this morning a report of the speech delivered last night by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson). Unfortunately I was able to hear only a small part of that speech. This report states;
Justice Minister Garson said last night in the Commons that Canada is not overtaxed and the government does not admit any large-scale extravagance or carelessness in the civil service.

The Address-Mr. Green
The heading is, "Canadians Said Not Overtaxed". I do not know where the Minister of Justice has been in recent months, or in recent years in fact. He is probably the only Canadian in the whole nation who does not believe that the Canadian people are being overtaxed. He is just that much behind the times.
We have a sales tax in Canada of 10 per cent, the highest in the history of the country. This tax is levied at the manufacturing level and then pyramids as it goes down to the level of the person making the purchase. We also have an income tax which is the highest we have ever had in peacetime, and which is making it extremely difficult for hundreds of thousands of Canadians to save for their old age. They are being placed in the position where they have to rely on security measures of one kind or another. Our corporation taxes are so high that there is not sufficient money available in Canada for the development of our resources, and billions of dollars must be brought in from the United States.
As I have said, a great portion of this money which is being taxed away from the Canadian people is devoted to the work of the Department of National Defence. Almost half of our budget for this current fiscal year is for the requirements of that department. I repeat that if there is one department of government which must be efficient at this time, it is the Department of National Defence.
I submit that the Canadian people and this House of Commons are entitled to a full statement of what the government proposes to do to remedy the defects outlined in the Currie report. Furthermore they are entitled to have immediate action taken to clean up this mess. So far we have had no such statement from any minister of the government. It would look as though all we are to get is a delayed explanation by a junior minister. In saying that I do not wish to belittle the minister in any way because he is a friend of many years' standing. He is also a neighbour and one of my constituents.
Does he vote for you?

I have not much hope of getting his support in the next election, but still I have to be a little careful. I repeat that this is not a job to be handled by a junior minister of the crown.	-
Steps should be taken at once to increase the efficiency of the defence department. That cannot be done successfully by the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). I say that for several reasons. He too is a man for whom I have a great deal of respect, but I think he has the wrong

portfolio. He has shown clearly that he is not sufficiently practical to clean up a mess of this kind. We need only refer to the report to find where he has been negligent, and I turn to page 712 of Hansard where we find this paragraph in the Currie report:
Before reciting the irregularities and their circumstances uncovered by the R.C.M.P.-with the assistance later of the provincial police and the army provost corps-it must be said-
These are the important words of the paragraph.
-that internal warnings had not been lacking in the Department of National Defence. The chief auditor of the department had performed his functions conscientiously. Time and again he had reported unsatisfactory conditions. This is clear from appendix "B" which summarizes his findings over a period of years. The deputy minister in each case had directed the quartermaster general to investigate and report. Lack of adequate action at this point had, however, caused a progressive deterioration in the situation. Aside from reports being delayed for considerable periods of time, the record shows the next audit revealing conditions similar to those previously reported and, in some cases, worse. The process is then again repeated.
What greater condemnation could there be of the Department of National Defence? What greater condemnation could there be of the deputy minister; and as such it must be taken as condemnation of the minister himself. Long ago he knew or should have known of these conditions, and he should have seen to it that they were cleaned up. If he had been an efficient, businesslike administrator he would have had them cleaned up.
Then I also suggest that the attitude of the minister is condemned in a paragraph on page 716 of Hansard. The minister was one of the higher-ups at least, and he certainly was at or near the top. The criticism contained in this paragraph must be taken as applying to him as well as to others. I think it is a perfectly accurate criticism of the minister. The heart of the paragraph is contained in the words, "costs count not at all." That has been the attitude of the minister. I am going to read the whole paragraph because I think it is a very reasonable statement of what we would expect. It reads as follows:
The situation was complicated by still another factor. The Department of National Defence (including the army works services) -
You will note that the army works services are only given attention by being included in brackets.
-was largely staffed and manned by men whose military training had been received in wartime. Its establishment and administrative practices reflected more clearly the urgent need and exigencies of war, when speed is everything and costs count not at all.

The Address-Mr. Green
By the way, the minister's training took place in that same period, and I suggest that he has the attitude referred to in this paragraph. I continue:
The carry-forward of this war psychology must be coupled with inadequate training and resultant ignorance on the part of personnel of their administrative duties and responsibilities. There was, in addition, indifference and reluctance on the part of military personnel to concentrate on administration to the degree required. It was not perhaps unnatural that these latter needs were largely forgotten or deliberately overlooked as soldiers gazed forward into the unknown consequences of the Korean outbreak, and foresaw still greater wars not very far away. But, if this spirit permeated the lower echelons of the army, it is more difficult to condone the same attitudes higher up.
In the unabridged or unrevised edition the words are "at or near the top."
There, a higher degree both of intelligence and responsibility is essential. It was not always present In the degree required.
' The original edition does not contain the word "always". The minister had exactly that same background and his faults were the same as those of the others who were involved. It is to that this reference is made. It is no wonder, Mr. Speaker, with this attitude that costs count not at all, that we find such heavy overpurchasing. We find tenders called for 62,000 serving forks. After protest is made we find that cut to 40,000 and then to 14,000. I hear now that the latest call for forks is only for 220, which is a great deal more in line with the number of serving or cooks' forks that are required. We have had the purchase of over a million pairs of shoes and all the other overpurchasing.
I prophesy that in the final analysis many of these things will be turned over to the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation to be sold at fire sale prices. I think the time has come when civilian goods of this kind should not be purchased in such large quantities, because if there should be a demand for them they can be made quickly by the existing industries. That is the trend now in the United States. In the United States News and World Report of December 5 I read a statement that they are planning now in the United States to set up reserve capacity to produce the requirements rather than manufacture the actual goods in such large quantities and then stockpile them, thereby probably bringing about obsolescence in many items and altogether a great waste of money.
Just last week I had one more example of the way the Department of National Defence has been carrying on. I have here the specifications that have been sent out to the tailors of Canada for the making of a peaked cap for air force officers. The document is called,
"Tailoring specification to guide private procurement." There are five written pages of specifications for air force officers' caps and two blueprints. Here I have the first blueprint, which has to do with the chin strap on the cap. There are half a dozen drawings on it. I do not know whether they go down' to the millionth of an inch, but they go down pretty small. All of the first blueprint has to do with the chin strap to go on the air force officers' peaked cap. I see that on the blueprint it says: "Note: tolerance: unless otherwise specified all fractional dimensions
of an inch." The blueprint of the chin strap is dated October 27, 1952 and is issued by the directorate of interservice development, Department of National Defence. There is a note on it to the effect that it has been drawn by one individual and that the order has been placed or approved-I cannot read' the word-by another. It is approved by another individual and checked by a third. That is the specification for a chin strap for an officer's cap. It looks like a machine gun specification.
There is here another specification, even larger, for the cap itself. There is a view of the cap from the north, east, south, and west -and it is also down to ^ or of an inch tolerance. It has also been checked by three different officials in this directorate of the Department of National Defence. Now, what earthly hope is there of having an efficient Department of National Defence when you have business carried on in that way?
I say further that the Minister of National Defence cannot organize this department efficiently because he has failed time and again to heed the warnings given in this house. Not only have they been given to him for years, but he has always answered that everything was all right; why were we worrying? It was all a lot of waste effort. His attitude in the house was so different from the attitude of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) when minister of national defence for air. In those days he came into this house and told us frankly what things were bothering him. He said: My department has been making mistakes in this regard and in that regard. I admit it. And he asked the members to help him out. He asked them to give him suggestions for ways in which those defects could be remedied; but there is nothing of that kind with the present Minister of National Defence. He does not admit errors, and he has been pitifully complacent about these warnings that have been given to his department.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is the one and only minister of the crown who

The Address-Mr. Drew can take adequate action to meet this situation. He and he alone can call for the minister's resignation; and what is required is a new minister. It is high time this Department of National Defence was put on a businesslike basis. Furthermore, the Canadian people are entitled to a statement by the Prime Minister on this Currie report. He cannot delegate his responsibility for explaining the government's stand to any other cabinet minister, and I hope he will give this house his views with regard to this whole question.
Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the
Opposition): Mr. Speaker, before the vote is taken on the amendment to the amendment I wish to deal with that motion and to indicate the course we propose to follow in regard to it.
The amendment to the amendment is put forward in the following motion:
That the amendment be amended by adding thereto the following:
"(f) To recommend legislation providing for the payment to producers, in respect of farm-stored grain, of an advance equal to 75 per cent of the initial price as established at August 1 in each crop year."
In dealing with the amendment now before us, it must be realized that the rules do not permit us to introduce any amendment to the wording of this subamendment. We must deal with it in its present form, whether we like that form or not.
In effect this subamendment does two things. It is a proposal that legislation be introduced to provide for a cash advance to producers in respect of their farm-stored grain equal to 75 per cent of the initial payment the producer would have received if he had been able to deliver that grain to an agency of the wheat board. The other effect of this resolution is to express want of confidence in the government in regard to their handling of the very large grain crop this year.
In view of the fact that farm storage of grain is not normal in Canada under ordinary circumstances when line elevator storage is available, it does not appear desirable that legislation should be designed to encourage farm storage when satisfactory elevator storage is a practical possibility. On the other hand it now seems necessary, and urgently necessary, that something be done to make cash available to the farmers for farm-stored grain, if they are to meet their current debts and make the necessary arrangements for the next year's crop. That is the principle at issue.
I emphasized this in my own remarks in the early stages of this debate on the speech from the throne. I would like to quote what
fMr. Green.1
I said on November 24 regarding this very subject, and I am reading from page 27 of Hansard:
The whole system of handling and distribution has broken down. The government, no matter what its explanation may be, has failed to take effective steps to provide for the handling of grain, in spite of the knowledge many months ago, and the warnings many months ago, that this situation was going to arise. In western Canada today there are many farmers, with huge quantities of wheat and other grains worth considerable sums of money, who are unable to get money at this time to cover their harvesting and living expenses because of their inability to deliver that grain to market.
This is a situation with which the government should deal immediately. It is urgent and calls for attention without delay.
As evidence of the fact that the government has not been meeting this situation, I would refer by way of illustration to the evidence furnished by a reply which was given today by the Department of Trade and Commerce. In response to a query as to the capacity of the dominion government grain elevator at Lethbridge, the answer shows that in November, which was the peak month this year for the handling of grain, that government grain elevator-at a time when there is such an accumulation of grain in western Canada-had only one-third of its actual capacity occupied. In the answer by the Department of Trade and Commerce the capacity of that elevator is given as 1,250,000 bushels, but in November there was stored in that elevator 457,161 bushels. That is merely evidence to support the statement that the government should be taking action to deal with this question.
For that reason we certainly support the purpose of this subamendment in principle. Legislation should be introduced to make cash available for grain which it has become necessary to store on the farms because of the abnormal conditions this year.
In dealing with the wording of any amendment or subamendment it is not possible to cross every "t" and dot every "i". We cannot vary the wording. Dealing with this subamendment strictly upon the basis of principle, we unhesitatingly support the proposal for legislation which will meet the urgent needs of the farmers of western Canada at this time, in accordance with what I have already said on behalf of our party at an earlier stage in this debate. On the ground, and recognizing that much more needs to be said in regard to the details of the legislation and the procedure by which this principle would become operative, all of which can be dealt with when the legislation is actually before us, we do propose to support this subamendment and hope that the government will accept the principle which it establishes, so the farmers of western Canada

may know that they are going to be able to meet the critical financial problems which confront them at this time.
The other feature of this subamendment is that it amounts to an expression of want of confidence in the government in regard to its handling of the present grain crop. From what we have already said there need be no doubt that we welcome the opportunity to express by our vote the strong criticism we believe should be directed against the government for their failure to deal with this situation which was so clearly anticipated many months in advance. With that matter I have already dealt in this debate. They have failed to take appropriate steps to meet a situation which had been openly discussed for a long time. They have failed to make transportation facilities available. They have failed to make arrangements under which the farmers can obtain the necessary cash for their daily requirements and their future production. On this ground we support the subamendment as an expression of criticism of the gross incompetence of the government in dealing with a situation which was apparent for a long time,

Mr. Speaker, before the vote is taken on this amendment to the amendment I feel that I should say a few words with regard to it. I am pleased that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has indicated that they will support the subamendment. As a matter of fact it is not asking for a great deal, if we consider the position of the wheat grower in the United States. We in western Canada farm under much the same conditions as do the wheat producers in the areas to the south of us. In the United States the wheat producers have what is known as a parity price for their wheat, based on the conditions which existed in that country from 1909 to 1914. Provision is made for a cash advance on farm-stored grain in the United States which is equal to 90 per cent of that parity price at the present time. That provision enables the farmer in the United States, under similar conditions, to obtain approximately $2 a bushel as an advance on farm-stored grain. In this amendment all we are asking is 75 per cent of the initial price of grain as determined by the government on August 1 of each year. On that basis, this year it would mean an advance payment of between 85 and 95 cents a bushel to the average producer in western Canada.
In view of the similarity between the conditions which exist in the two largest wheat-producing areas in the world, we feel that in western Canada we should have somewhat similar treatment. The fact that this or some
The Address-Mr. Wright similar payment is not made available means that in the fall of the year many of the producers in western Canada, in order to get cash to meet their obligations which come due in the fall, are obliged to sacrifice some other product which they produce. Quite often this takes the form of selling their livestock; and that is what has taken place over the last number of years. The farmer has not enough money available, under the initial payment and the quota, to meet his obligations. He is therefore obliged to sacrifice his livestock. That is one of the reasons we get congestion in our livestock market in the fall of the year, with the result that at that time prices to the producer are demoralized.
When I was in western Canada this fall we were marketing first-grade beef cattle at from 18 cents to 21 cents a pound, where they were under the weights required. Under the floor price legislation which was provided for beef at that time, an animal had to dress 700 pounds. There in western Canada, as I said, I saw first-grade beef cattle weighing from 1,000 to 1,200 pounds live weight, and dressing from 500 to 600 pounds, being sold for 18 cents to 21 cents a pound. After I came down east here to attend the session of parliament I happened to be on a farm in eastern Ontario, and the farmer showed me a return which he had received that day on a three-year-old Holstein steer which he had sold, and which weighed 1,600 pounds. He received 25 cents a pound for it. He received in the neighbourhood of $400 for an inferior beef animal which we were selling in western Canada, dressing somewhat less, for in the neighbourhood of $200.
If some provision were made whereby cash could be made available to farmers in Canada as suggested in this subamendment, I am certain that it would prevent chaotic conditions in the marketing of other agricultural products in the fall of the year. I see no reason why it cannot be done. It is all right for the government to say that the farmer can go to a bank and get money if he needs it, when he has good marketable grain in store on his farm. But there are many farmers, especially the smaller ones, who over the years have had little dealings with the banks. It is all right for the large farmer who has a section or two of land. He has probably had dealings with banking institutions over the years, and he can obtain the credit that is necessary to carry on in an emergency. The smaller farmer, however, the man who has not had dealings with the bank and whom the banker does not know, finds it exceedingly difficult to obtain the necessary credit.
I do not intend to press this matter further, but I think the government should give

Mr. Speaker, before
addressing my remarks to the Petawawa incident and some related matters, I should like to dispose of the question that has been raised from time to time, I think twice yesterday, with respect to the retirement of Brigadier Connelly. I should like to do this by reading to the members of the house a statement prepared by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) which reads as follows:
Hon. members are well aware of the confidential nature of the relationship which must exist between the Minister of National Defence and his service advisers.
The head of each of the armed services is responsible for the efficiency of his service and it is part of that responsibility to make recommendations regarding the retention or retirement of officers having regard to the best interests of the service.
The chief of the general staff recommended to me that Brigadier Connelly should be retired and after discussing the matter with the chief of the general staff I felt that the retention of Brigadier Connelly would not be in the interests of the services or of the public and therefore approved the recommendation.
This retirement was dealt with entirely as a military matter and the Secretary of State for External Affairs had nothing whatever to do with it in any way.
That is the end of the minister's statement.
I have listened throughout the past few days with very great interest to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and his followers in their attempts to indict the Minister of National Defence and embarrass the government by playing up a relatively small matter into one in which they seek to involve the whole of the army and the whole of the Department of National Defence. The basis on which they seek to raise this amazing superstructure is the activities of a few crooks and thieves at Petawawa who stole and converted to their own use equipment and stores at the army works services depot there. By exaggeration and by irresponsible statements and unreasonable deductions, they have in my opinion succeeded in working themselves into considerable hysteria politically, which political hysteria they seek to pass on to the people of this country. Maybe that is just
The Address-Mr. Campney another way of saying that they appear to be endeavouring to play politics with the Currie report.

-to have the situation
reduced to its proper proportions and dealt with coolly and factually, and with due regard to the use of words and some sense of proportion. The situation at Petawawa arose primarily from the operations of certain crooks, some of them within the service and some of them civilians outside the service, who conspired together to steal and convert and turn to their own use certain stores and equipment at Petawawa.
I should like briefly to run over the narrative of that phase of the matter. I might say that in the late summer of 1951 the provost corps, the inspector of quartermasters' services and the auditor general's representative in checking over the situation at Petawawa, which was growing in activity at a tremendous rate, found some minor irregularities. They were not very great ones, but they were sufficient to lead them to be reported to the department. That report was under consideration and remedial measures were also under consideration when the letter referred to in Mr. Currie's report was received. That was in October.
As soon as this letter was received the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were asked immediately by the minister to make a thorough and complete examination of the situation at Petawawa. This the R.C.M.P. proceeded to do, assisted by the officers of the provost corps.
By February of 1952 sufficient information had been accumulated to indicate that a conspiracy did in fact exist, as I have inti-
862	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Campney mated, and that individuals additional to those at first suspected were implicated in the conspiracy and theft. The minister immediately appointed local counsel, and later appointed Mr. J. W. Pickup, Q.C., now chief justice of the high court of Ontario, as senior counsel. Prosecutions were launched and that was announced by the minister in the House of Commons on April 21 last.
Those prosecutions were launched as promptly as the accumulated facts warranted and were pressed to conclusion as speedily as the processes of the courts would permit. Five military personnel and ten civilians were charged. Of the five military personnel, two were officers and three were non-commissioned officers. Four of the five military personnel were convicted and sentenced, as were eight of the ten civilians. In addition, disciplinary action was taken against a certain number of other military personnel as well.
The evidence adduced at the trials indicated that a fairly comprehensive system of collusion had been worked out between those within the service and those without. That is why it probably took longer than would ordinarily have been the case where a straight theft had occurred, to correlate the information and ensure that the guilty persons might be punished. That in brief is the story of the criminal side of the Petawawa matter.
I submit that in all the steps in that connection the minister acted with dispatch, the department acted with dispatch and the guilty people were in fact punished. I do not think there is anything very earth-shaking in that, because thefts do occur and conspiracies do occur. They occur in all phases of our day to day life. Because a bank is robbed, you do not seek to indict the president. Because gold is stolen from a mine, you do not start out by arresting all the directors.
These things happen. Nobody likes them; nobody approves of them, but they take place. The fallibility of human nature is not confined to any particular class of people or to any particular area. Yet from the strictures which I have heard, especially yesterday and today, it would appear that it is sought by opposition members to hold the Minister of National Defence liable for all these incidents of stealing, petty thieving and pilfering which occur throughout the tremendous properties, buildings and areas which the Department of National Defence operates. So far as the thefts at Petawawa are concerned, while nobody condones them, and certainly nobody approves of them, they were not as a matter of fact in the aggregate of very great magnitude-

The police, too, have been able to recover by far the greater quantity of the missing goods, and these have been returned to stores.
It seems to me that what I have stated is a fair and complete record of the thieving itself and of the incidents that took place at Petawawa. The situation was a local one and would ordinarily be treated as such and dealt with by the police and the criminal courts. There is no new evidence cited in the report that was not available in the criminal courts, and that was not used there. In short, all the incidents to which Mr. Currie refers by way of evidence, as it were, took place in 1950 and early 1951, and were all public property a long time ago.
But there is another side of the Petawawa matter, and I should now like to address myself to that. I refer to the question of the operations of the Department of National Defence at Petawawa. Coincidentally with the minister authorizing the appointment of counsel, the launching of prosecutions and the criminal proceedings at Petawawa, in view of the extent to which these things seemed to have prevailed from the information that had been gleaned, involving, as I said, five military personnel and ten civilians, the minister took the view that he ought to have the whole situation reviewed apart from the criminal prosecutions to see what was the situation at Petawawa within the departmental picture. Accordingly he appointed Mr. George Currie to make a complete investigation. I should like to quote a few sentences from the minister's statement in the

house on April 21 when he announced the appointment of Mr. Currie. He said:
-I have engaged Mr. George S. Currie, chartered accountant of Montreal, a former deputy minister of national defence, to make a full investigation of the situation, security and accounting procedure for engineer stores, equipment and services at Petawawa and elsewhere . . . Everything possible will be done to get to the bottom of this situation and take such action and adopt such remedies as may be required.
I should like to observe in passing that the appointment of Mr. Currie was made by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Clax-ton), and was not made by the house or by the government. His appointment was made at the instance of the minister in an effort to find out what the situation was at Petawawa with a view to having that situation remedied. As I will develop a little later, by reason of the fact that Mr. Currie was appointed and engaged by the minister he worked with officials of the Department of National Defence. They worked with him. Everybody was interested in finding out what had really happened to permit a conspiracy of members of the service with outside civilians to develop at Petawawa. If the minister had been so disposed, I think he might very well have regarded Mr. Currie's report as a document privileged to him, but he did not take that view. He never did take that view.
On the other hand he never said in the house in any statement he made that he would table the report or that he would regard it as a parliamentary document. I am not raising the issue and I am not arguing it; I am merely saying the fact is that he caused the Currie report to be tabled voluntarily because he felt that members of the house should know what the situation was. I think in doing so he showed courage, although he has incurred certain opprobrium from the members of the opposition by reason of what was in the report. I want it to be clear on the record that the report was made by a man engaged by the minister as a minister.
Between the date of the appointment of Mr. Currie and the filing of his report Mr. Currie was given access, and properly so, to all records of the department and of the army works services and depots, and to all the information and assistance from the officials of both that he desired. The result was that he made a survey and a study not only of Petawawa, where the incident which provided the occasion for his appointment arose, but of army works service units at Toronto, London, Camp Borden, Barriefield, Vancouver, Regina, Quebec and Halifax. He visited army works service depots, studied their situations and based a report thereon.
The Address-Mr. Campney
He came to certain conclusions with respect to army works services in general and with respect to Petawawa in particular. His conclusions were in the first place that there had been some break-down in administration, supervision, accounting and security in the depots operated by the army works services, and I propose to deal with that a little later. He also stated, as indicated at page 2 of his report, that notwithstanding the fact that he did not think operations were all that could be desired, only at Petawawa were there any substantial losses from the irregularities. This is what he had to say:
It does not fit the facts to indict or to smear the whole army works services personnel because of the sins of a handful of crooks.
So far as I know he found no other handful of crooks than those at Petawawa, and he studied all depots throughout the country.

So far as his general recommendations and findings are concerned, he also stated that the system of accounting would seem to be a proper one but that it was not operated properly, and I should like to make some comment on that. Before I do so, I should like to deal for a moment-because I think we should look at these things practically and realistically-with the army works services, what they were and what happened to them in two or three years.
The army works services are chiefly maintenance units, small in size, which look after running maintenance and minor construction at army camps throughout the country. In most cases up until Korea or just before their work was not relatively very extensive. For example, at Petawawa camp in 1947 the army works services were on a sort of caretaker basis. It was a big camp, but they had about 100 personnel and spent probably $100,000 a year in maintenance of that camp. Now, as is indicated in Mr. Currie's report-and of course verified by the figures from the department-that has all changed. As he states at page 16 of the report:
During the 1952-53 period, the Petawawa detachment will expend something in excess of $1 million on its own account, as well as having administrative responsibility for supervising some $20 million of new construction-
In other words, from spending $100,000 per annum in five years that unit had to take care of spending $1 million and supervising another $20 million, while its personnel has increased from about 100 to between 400 and 500. I think any practical person will realize -in civil life or in army life; it doesn't matter-that to step up an organization from 100 to nearly 500 or we will say 450, and from spending $100,000 to spending $1 million

The Address-Mr. Campney per year and supervising the expenditure of $20 million per year as well is a big increase in duties and responsibilities in a short period of time. The difficulties that would be encountered in finding suitable technical people would be, and have continually been one of the most serious problems of the Department of National Defence ever since the expansion of the army started.
At Petawawa today we have two complete regiments with all ancillary services, over 4,500 people. We have a huge establishment that has to be looked after by the army works services.
I would now like to make a few observations with respect to what I said about Mr. Currie's statement that the accounting system seems to be all right but that it was not operated properly.

I would like to make a few observations on that. In 1948 the Department of National Defence itself made an intensive study of the army works services and of the accounting and supervising system. A complete reorganization was effected, and now we have 16 works companies with 33 detachments distributed throughout Canada from Vancouver to Newfoundland and from the north to the south of Canada. V/e have a personnel of about 7,500. It was intended that this system of accounting and supervision would be introduced into the army works service units in 1950 and 1951 as fast as suitable personnel could be obtained. Mr. Currie, at page 12 of his report, recognizes the efficacy of this system when he says- and it is this system to which he is referring:
The fault did not lie in the accounting system, which was a good one had it been operated properly.
I want to make some remarks on that later.
It was a new system, based on American and British as well as Canadian experience, and embodied features which, theoretically, would have quickly checked irregularities as they appeared.
He also says:
The accounting system, however, was not properly operated, nor were the regulation inventories methodically carried out.
That is true and there are reasons for it. The reaction on the part of any member or any citizen would be: Why was not the accounting system carried out? I think that is a fair and reasonable question, and it is a question that should be answered. I will try, in my humble way, to give an answer to that question, although Mr. Currie almost does it for me on page 15 of his report when he says:
-the problems, difficulties and shortcomings of the army works services outlined above-


which he had dealt with-
__suggest that they have been caused for the most
part-but by no means altogether-by the tremendous and sudden expansion of its activities brought about by the Korean war and by the large scale defence program involved in carrying out our NATO activities.
Again he says:
The establishment approved for the army works services after the second world war did not envisage the sudden expansion which was to take place in 1950. It was designed to carry out a purely peacetime role of planning, development and construction on an annual expenditure of approximately $20 million. This establishment became quickly burdened under the impact of big scale rearmament. In September, 1950, the program was increased to about $80 million. In the following April, it was increased to about $200 million. The program envisaged in the 1952-53 fiscal year aggregates about $250 million. Tne magnitude of this responsibility is reflected in an investment in plant and buildings which now amounts to $750 million and is still rising.
The question which follows from that- because after all that is an enormous expansion-is, why could not the army keep up with the rapid expansion? Civilian industry cannot do it always, although it does do it sometimes. The pertinent question in my mind, and I think in the minds of all members, is why could they not keep up with it. Well, I should like to say that there are probably three reasons why the army was not able to keep up with that expansion. The first reason is, I think, the root of some of the difficulties that have been encountered in the army works services. The army works service depends, as far as its direction is concerned, on engineers and accountants. They must be available and they must be on hand at all those depots, and they must be competent and trained.
As the demand by the army for engineers and accountants grew, the civilian demand for the same people was also growing. As between the army and the civilian industry of this country, the civilian industry is not bound by any particular restrictions or regulations. They go out, and nobody can complain of it, and pay any price to get what they go after-if they can afford it. Now, the army has to operate on regulations, on rank, and on salaries and allowances. They cannot go out and get a captain of engineers today and pay him what they have to pay him, and then go out and get another one tomorrow and pay him something different. They have to operate within a framework. The same thing applies to their civilian supervisors such as accountants. In that connection, and I do not say so with any disparagement, they also have sitting over them a body known as the civil service commission. The civil service commission has its categories for accountants and it has its salary

range. As far as I can tell from looking quickly at the relevant figures, an engineer entering the armed services from college, or an accountant after his graduation, will take about five years to arrive at the point from which he could start in very many commercial industries.
That is a real problem, and you do not solve it by drawing something out of a hat. The department had to do the best it could and it had to try and train a lot of people itself. The department did try to train them while work was piling up and piling up still higher. As reasonable people, can hon. members imagine how much time the meagre staff we had in those depots had for training other people while they were also carrying out duties many times in excess of those which they had ever carried out before? That was the problem the department had to cope with.

I am not ruling that factor out because the fallibility of people also has a bearing. When you have to get a large number of people in a hurry you cannot be quite so particular about the type of people you get; and the people you get, whether they are on the civilian side of the department or in the army, are just like everybody else; they are good, bad and indifferent. You do not get all perfect people; because whether it is an army unit or in the civilian services of the Department of National Defence, there are always a few people who go wrong. But who does not have such people? Commercial companies have them. Every department of government has them. You cannot avoid that.
I would ask hon. members to keep in mind at all times that while we were trying to solve these problems there was a continual burden being thrust upon the army works services which in some cases was almost fantastic as compared with what they had had to do two or three years previously. That is a real problem for anybody to try to solve. I do not think any reasonable man will fail to recognize the effect of that problem on the development of a large service in a short 68108-55
