Mr. Speaker, I did not speak during the debate on the address in reply at the beginning of the sixth session of the 21st parliament. I preferred to comment on some of the bills brought before the house during the session. For this reason without further delay I would like today to congratulate the government for having complied with the legitimate wishes of all our compatriots by appointing a Canadian to the highest and most representative position in the country. Inasmuch as I am permitted to do so by the rules of the house, in the name of the electors I represent and in my own name, I respectfully congratulate the Right Hon. Vincent Massey upon his appointment as the first of a long line of Canadian-born viceroys.
The matter is not a new one. It had been discussed for a long time and this wonderful appointment was made in due course. All those whose love goes first to Canada who want to be Canadians above all were pleased with it. I said a moment ago that the matter was not a new one. Indeed, several years ago, in 1935, Mr. Maurice Ollivier, law clerk of the House of Commons, in his prophetical book, "Le Canada, pays souverain", wrote:
The letters patent appointing a governor should be replaced by revised letters patent appointing a viceroy who should be Canadian.
Why not avail ourselves of our status of full equality and fulfil the legitimate aspirations arising from our emancipation.
The appointment of a Canadian would symbolize the growth, the increasing independence of Canada.
Moreover, the appointment of a Canadian would be an excellent thing for Great Britain who would cease to be blamed unfairly for the mistakes of the representative of the sovereign.
The British empire of yesterday is now a commonwealth of nations bound by common economic interests.
It is with extreme pleasure that I congratulate the mover of the address in reply, my very good friend the member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Deslieres), whose constituency is next to mine, and a very beautiful constituency at that. I know this from experience since I spent with the new member the trying days of his electoral campaign. You can

see now that he carried this campaign to a victorious conclusion. I must add to these congratulations a tribute to the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Schneider) who discharged, as expected, in a wonderful manner the task with which he had been entrusted.
Mr. Speaker, we are now at the stage where the last vestiges of colonialism are going by the board. For several years now we have enjoyed the right to govern ourselves, that is to adopt the legislation which suits us best without taking into account the legislation of any other country. We have indeed obtained the right to negotiate alone our own treaties. We have obtained the right to a distinctive diplomatic representation abroad. We have abolished the right of appeal to the privy council, not only in criminal cases but in every other case as well. Our sovereignty is now complete. There remains, it is true, the right to amend the constitution, and on that point I should like to congratulate the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), as well as the government, for having obtained in 1949, on behalf of the federal parliament the right to amend our constitution in federal matters, a right that the provinces themselves have enjoyed since 1867 in provincial matters.
There remains only to obtain the right for Canada and its provinces to amend the constitution in those matters that relate both to federal and provincial rights. This, however, would not affect our autonomy, our sovereignty, for the simple reason that Britain would be only too glad to have the Canadian constitution, that is the B.N.A. Act of 1867, put completely into our hands.
It remains only for us to come to an agreement with the provinces on a method of amendment which would satisfy everyone, and which would protect at the same time federal and provincial rights, as well as minority rights which are exceedingly important to us. As a matter of fact, one should not forget that the federal members from the province of Quebec in Ottawa represent their province here as well as the provincial members, and that, like them, they are devoted to the tongue, traditions and customs of their ancestors.
However they do not forget that they have a sacred duty: not only must they be nationalists or provincialists but, above all, they must be Canadians. Quebec is our native land, but the whole of Canada belongs to us, it is our
The Address-Mr. Boivin larger mother country; why should we, therefore, erect a wall around the province of Quebec, in order to isolate it from the rest of the world and, more particularly, from the rest of Canada?
Canada is a great country, a truly beautiful country; it is a land abounding in all riches and all beauties, from the St. Lawrence river to the Rocky mountains, and across the golden western plains. The whole country is our inheritance and what a shame it would be if we ever had the idea of transforming it into a sort of Balkan area, when ten distinct provinces would each be led by some petty dictator, who would deem himself free to manage everything to his own liking and solely to his own advantage.
I am bound to say that my patriotism oversteps somewhat the boundaries of my province, though I retain strong ties with the land where I was born, with that province whose faith, language and traditions I shall always uphold whatever the circumstances. I am still happy to be a citizen of a great and beautiful country and to assert that I am a Canadian.
I take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage) on the masterful speech he made on this matter, on December 2 last.
Mr. Speaker, there is another subject about which I should like to say a few words, as it is linked with the first: namely communism. In principle, we all agree that communism is our greatest, our most dangerous and most insidious enemy, an enemy that threatens and seeks to destroy us. There are many ways of fighting it. The first and easiest way is to denounce it, but unfortunately that is not sufficient and we must take other means, that is prepare ourselves to fight that enemy.
Russia has been arming and mobilizing her military forces for a long time now. What will be the use of our oratory if we are not ready to clash on the day of decision, with the communists, with equal forces or preferably with superior forces.
What will be the use of all our prosperity, of our wealth, of all the institutions we will have set up, of all the houses we will have built, of all the automobiles we will have manufactured and of all the tractors or other agricultural implements we will have placed at the disposal of our agricultural people, if we are to be invaded one day, Mr. Speaker, by these barbarians who are watching us on the
872	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Boivin other side of the Arctic. All these achievements, all that wealth would be taken away from us and we would be reduced to slavery by an hostile power.
It is true that taxes are high, but it is a small price to pay for liberty. Our freedom is more precious than all our wealth; these millions that we are spending on national defence are very little after all, although they may sometimes weigh heavily on our shoulders, compared with the safety they afford and guarantee. In other words, taxes are an evil, but a necessary evil, and are to be preferred to the evils that would befall us if, due to a lack of preparedness, we were to be shorn like sheep in the slaughterhouse.
All these taxes for national defence, all this revenue is provided by direct taxation, that is by personal and corporation income tax. Should we leave this field to the provinces and open our country to invasion?
If I may say so, Mr. Speaker-and I believe you will agree with me-should our country be invaded and conquered by the barbarians who live under communist rule, there would hardly be any more discussion of federal or provincial or minority rights. There would be little talk of the Christian religion, of our language and of our traditions.
That is what must be understood whenever there is any discussion over the apportionment of fields of taxation between the federal government and the provinces. I sincerely believe that the defence of this country and the survival of our nation are more important even than highway construction, important though that may be.
While we are on this subject, I must add that we should come to the assistance of those who need our help, who are hungry. I am referring to those countries which live in the shadow of communism.
One must admit that we have now in our warehouses a surplus of meat and that we have to pay for such storage in order not to lose this meat. So why not distribute this meat to those who are on the verge of rebellion or of falling prey to these barbarians? We would thus give them a foretaste of the real sense of democracy.
Mr. Speaker, having referred to income tax,
I should like to repeat the request I made in this house on May 27 last, in connection with the worker's income tax. I believe very sincerely that the father of a family as well as the individual, with the present cost of 

living, is not sufficiently compensated by way of basic exemptions. In this connection, I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) to the manner in which income tax collectors and their staffs go about collecting amounts which are in arrears of one, two or even three years. A letter is sent advising them that if the amount is not paid within fifteen days, a garnishee order will be issued and sent to the employer.
With the present cost of living, the ordinary worker finds it very difficult to meet his obligations and that is why in many instances, if the Minister of National Revenue institutes proceedings against them, that represents for these people a real catastrophe. I hope that my brief remarks on that subject will urge the Minister of National Revenue to convene his collectors in order to ask them, or at least recommend to them, to be a little more lenient, as well as remind them that they are our servants.
I am convinced that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), together with his advisers, can and must find other means of levying revenues for his needs, if such is the case, without inflicting so much harm on those I have mentioned.
Mr. Speaker, I now come to a subject to which I have already referred in the past. On March 19 last, I wrote a long letter to the Minister of Finance concerning taxes on cigarettes. I should like to discuss this matter during the few minutes I still have at my disposal. It is true that the last budget brought a reduction of three cents on a package of cigarettes, or of $1.50 a thousand.
I	remember that the minister had informed us that he had received a lot of free advice concerning this tax. I should like to tell you right now that I never gave any advice. I must admit though that had I been one of his financial advisers I would have liked to give him a bit of advice. Possibly the tax on cigarettes would not be what it is today. I have already asked him in the past to cut
II	cents off the tax-that was before the last reduction-not including of course Mr. Duplessis' additional 4 cents. This would have brought the price of our domestic cigarettes down to 35 cents.
Mr. Speaker, it must be admitted that approximately 50 per cent of our people smoke smuggled American cigarettes which they buy for 30 cents a pack, in order to save

money. A pack of Canadian cigarettes would cost 43 cents-that is with Mr. Duplessis' 4 cent tax-and you cannot blame them too much, in view of the present high cost of living.
With your permission I would like to make a survey going back to 1932 when cigarettes sold for 20 cents a pack. At that time, as will be remembered, there was an excise tax of $4 per thousand and a sales tax of 4 per cent. With these figures for 1932 in our minds, let us come now, if you wish, to the figures for 1952. Cigarettes are now sold here at 39 cents a pack, not including the Quebec tax. We must not overlook the fact that the excise tax has jumped to $10 per thousand and that the sales tax has been increased to 10 per cent. Let us say that the increase in taxation is the basic factor in the price increase of our Canadian cigarettes.
Considering that the per capita consumption of cigarettes in 1941 was 746 cigarettes in Canada and comparing it with the American per capita consumption during the same year, we find that the latter was 1,575 cigarettes. In 1942, the Canadian excise tax was increased by $2 per 1,000 and, during the same year, in the United States, consumption increased by 200 to reach the figure of 1,775 cigarettes per person. In 1943, the $2 increase in the Canadian excise tax had the effect of increasing the per capita consumption in the United States to 1,925.
So, Mr. Speaker, realizing gradually that the price of our cigarettes was much too high, our people have been buying more and more American cigarettes. This is the cause of the gradual increase in the per capita consumption of American cigarettes in the United States, which reached 2,400 cigarettes in 1950.
I have no figures for 1951, but I am sure they are still higher, because we see more and more smuggled cigarettes in Canada. The figures I have quoted are based on American production and they prove once again that per capita consumption in the United States is much higher than it should actually be, because of Canadian purchases of smuggled cigarettes.
The Minister of Finance stated during the last session that the volume of cigarette smuggling had been exaggerated. I am wondering whether he was not alluding to the statements I had made in the house when I said that four out of every five people were smoking American cigarettes. I am not the only one 68108-56
The Address-Mr. Boivin who thinks so. To corroborate my statements, I would like to quote an article from the Revue de Granby entitled "Between the lines" and dated April 5, 1952. I quote:
The budget brought down by the Hon. Mr. Abbott, who is hoping for a $9 million surplus in 1952-1953, will certainly not help police officers in their fight against the smuggling of American cigarettes. Citizens of the eastern townships will surely stop smoking Canadian cigarettes which cost 13 cents more per pack of 20 and continue to buy their smokes on the black market. Local club and hotel waiters tell us that 8 or 9 empty packages of cigarettes out of 10 left on tables by their customers are of American brands.
After reading that article we must come to the conclusion that some of our people think nothing of smuggling, as may be seen any day. On March 15, the Montreal Star published an item entitled "A judge tolerates smuggling". I quote:
Mr. Justice R. Herbert Barton stated yesterday that smuggling of American cigarettes into Canada was not too serious a matter. During the hearing in Toronto police court of a case involving a taxi driver whose car had been seized because he had smuggled American cigarettes, the judge said: That is only smuggling and everybody is doing it.
When a judge makes statements of that nature, I believe it is high time for the Minister of Finance to take action and reduce the tax.
I am convinced that the reduction of $1.50 per thousand, or 3 cents per package, has not brought about the increase in sales of Canadian cigarettes anticipated by the minister. Unfortunately, smuggling continues to the prejudice of Canadian manufacturers and of our national revenue.
I would like to quote here from an editorial which I found in La Voix de VEst of Granby, dated April 10, 1952, which bears out my contention:
As for cigarettes, we believe that a three cent reduction is ridiculous and that Mr. Abbott should have reduced the price to 35 cents per pack of twenty cigarettes with a view to increasing the consumption in Canada. It is evident that, as a result of the budget speech, the smuggling of cigarettes will soar again, because a great many Canadians will refuse to pay 43 cents for a pack of cigarettes they are able to purchase for 27 or 30 cents.
In the face of all this evidence, one has to admit that the excise tax reduction which I suggested would have reduced both smuggling and per capita consumption of cigarettes in the United States and lead to an increase in Canadian consumption. We like to smoke cigarettes as much as the Americans do; we smoke as many as they do. How can you explain that consumption in the United States is twice as high as in Canada? The explanation is simple. It lies in the difference between the excise tax in the two countries. In the United States the excise tax, for 1952, was $4 per thousand whereas in Canada, even

The Address-Mr. Boivin after the $1.50 reduction, it remains at $10 plus a sales tax of 10 per cent.
I do hope that we may cut down this far-famed excise tax when the time comes to bring down the budget. If we reduce this tax we will allow for the sale of cigarettes at a reasonable price. Moreover we will reduce smuggling and, by the same token, increase our own production and consumption.
Mr. Speaker, it is true that our manufacturers are subject to an abnormally high tax considering the price of their product, but I really believe it would be wrong to think that they would take advantage of a reduction in the excise tax to increase their profit. I really believe that the people of this country should not be left under a false impression, after the words spoken in this house by the hon. member from Bow River (Mr. Johnston) at the last session. That is why I would like to call your attention once more to the figures I mentioned a few minutes ago, while adding others in order to support my contention. 1932: retail price, 20 cents, excise tax, $4 a thousand, sales tax 4 per cent; 1952: retail price, 39 cents, excise tax, $10 a thousand, sales tax 10 per cent.
Since companies have, as you know, cartons of various sizes for sale to wholesalers, I shall take for comparison purposes the sale price of 100 cigarettes. In 1932, 100 cigarettes in 20-cigarette packs represented five packs at 20 cents, that is $1, excise tax of $4 a thousand, that is 40 cents, sales tax of 4 per cent or 1-3 cents, commission to jobbers, 10-5 cents, commission on retail sales, 17 cents.
The 100 cigarettes which sold for $1 in 1932, cost in taxes and commissions 68-8 cents; the manufacturer's selling price was therefore 31-2 cents or $1.12 for a carton of 18 packs of 20 cigarettes. For the purpose of my comparison-, I shall now take the retail price of 1952 which is 39 cents. Five packs at 39 cents, retail price, represent the sum of $1.95, the excise tax at $10 a thousand, $1.00, the sales tax at 10 per cent, 6 cents, the jobber's commission, 12-2 cents, the commission on retail sales, 22 cents, or a total of $1,404-
Cigarettes which sold at $1.95 a hundred in 1952 are costing, in taxes and commissions, $1,404, the manufacturer's sale price therefore being 54-8 cents or $1.97 a carton.
It seems to me odd indeed to hear people criticize the manufacturers' profits, without knowing the facts. The cigarette manufacturers have, within the last 20 years, raised their price by 23-6 cents for one hundred cigarettes and by 85 cents for a carton.


Let us keep in mind that raw leaf tobacco for cigarettes sold for 20-5 cents a pound in 1932, whereas, in 1951, it had more than doubled and cost 44-5 cents a pound. The raw products of the cigarette industry number a thousand and more and they have also followed the mounting trend of raw leaf tobacco prices. Further, we must allow for the fact that the cost of living has also increased for the cigarette manufacturers from 1932 to 1952. Within the last 20 years, they have raised the wholesale price, and not their profits by 85 cents a carton, and yet the manufacturers are being accused of increasing their profits, when the government has, by means of taxation, raised the price of these products by $1.97 a carton. The cost of living index had reached 190-4 per cent in October 1951, at the time when the raise of two cents mentioned took place. The cost of living had also gone up for the employees, who had obtained repeated salary increases. One of these sister industries is established in our district; I am in a position to state that its employees are well treated, both from the standpoint of salary and of security for themselves and their families. That is why I deemed it necessary to reply in the house to certain accusations made here by another hon. member, who made them with no ill intent, I trust.
I can only express once again the hope that the excise tax will be lowered so that Canadian cigarettes may sell for 35 cents retail. Then, for the small difference, our people will certainly smoke Canadian cigarettes. The increase in production will make up for the difference in national revenue so that it would be approximately the same as today.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate my colleague, the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) who more than 25 years ago sat with my late father in parliament.
I wish also to congratulate very sincerely the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) for the appointment of a citizen of Granby to the commission due to sail for South America on January 5.
Indeed, the city of Granby last week held a banquet to honour the general manager of the Granby co-operative who will be leaving shortly. I believe that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has found the most competent man in the province of Quebec in the person of the manager of the Granby Agricultural Co-operative. This is, to be sure, not only a tribute to the city of Granby, but to all the farmers of Quebec.
Before resuming my seat, Mr. Speaker, I would also like to offer my most sincere congratulations to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) who has finally given the city of Granby a long awaited post office building.

Mr. Speaker, I thank you very much for your indulgence.

Therefore if any further information is required, and I believe there is, the only way to get that information-and that is the way this information was obtained -is by appointing a commissioner who is free from the political associations that are inevitably connected with anything of this kind that is done here.
May I say in regard to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) that he has taken, and very properly, a serious view of this report. In every word and in his attitude one could see that he is concerned; but the Acting Minister of National Defence made light of the whole thing tonight. He said nothing really of importance had happened; that nearly all of the recommendations, or in any case a great many of them, that were made in the report had already been put into effect. There is one answer to that, sir, and it is this. If the commissioner-and I hope I am using the proper term in regard to Mr. Currie-was not able to find in the department the result of those recommendations that the acting minister said had already been put into effect, of what advantage was it to put them into effect? Surely, just for the sake of making them he would not have made recommendations in regard to a condition which he had

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis found had already been remedied by the administration. That makes nonsense of the whole report; and the report is not nonsense.
The Acting Minister of National Defence read this statement-and I assure him that this was taken out of its context:
No reliable estimate of the total loss can be prepared. It does, however, appear probable that the total loss resulting from misappropriations and irregularities by military personnel at Petawawa was not large.
Then the paragraph goes on:
My view would be, however, that the generally lax administrative situation would give rise to waste and inefficiency far more costly in loss than that covered by actual dishonesty. The evidence examined does not disclose irregularities involving relatively large sums of money, but, rather, an impressive array of petty irregularities on an extensive scale.
Here the Acting Minister of National Defence quoted five lines taken out of their context, while the rest of the paragraph was as damaging to the administration as anything could be. May I ask whether that was done for political purposes or not?
Then we go further back; I cannot give the pages as they are in the report itself and I am reading from the text in Hansard. The Acting Minister of National Defence said: If a bank is robbed, surely one would not blame the president for the loss of the money, or words to that effect. But if the president or the manager left the door of the bank open, surely he would be subject to criticism for doing so, and that is exactly what was done by the Department of National Defence.
The acting minister went on to say that though there were camps at Toronto, London, Borden, Barriefield, Vancouver, Regina, Quebec and Halifax, no maladministration was found in those places, or no petty thieving of the kind that was found at Petawawa. But Mr. Currie said far more than that. He said:
The conclusion I have come to is that, while there has been a general breakdown in the system of administration, supervision and accounting, it was only at Petawawa that extensive irregularities over a prolonged period of time took place. The contents of this chapter are chiefly based upon my studies there, because of the existence there of a combination of factors: lax control, poor discipline and the presence of dishonest personnel. The combination proved disastrous.
The Acting Minister of National Defence glossed it all over as though it were of no particular importance whatsoever. Then he went on to take another few lines out of their context. He read this:
It does not fit the facts to indict or to smear the whole army works services personnel because of the sins of a handful of crooks.
But he did not go on to read:
At Petawawa, however, the crooks were present and took advantage of the situation, and it is an unhappy circumstance that the beginning of this

investigation lies not inside the Department of National Defence and its full complement of regulations and supervising personnel, but with the receipt of an anonymous letter couched in the following terms:
Had it not been for the fact that someone took the trouble to write to the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, so far as the Department of National Defence is concerned these things would be going on yet. Surely, Mr. Speaker, under conditions of that kind the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) is open to criticism. And it is sheer impudence for anyone to come here and talk on his behalf and say that he is not. Either he is responsible for what has happened or no one has responsibility at all in matters of this kind.
So I would suggest to hon. members on both sides of the house that, while we cannot altogether get away from political associations in parliamentary procedures, for the good of Canada and for the morale and good of the men who are now serving in the forces and who are carrying out their duties under most difficult circumstances, we should not allow such things as happened at Petawawa to go by without placing the blame where it should be placed, showing the people of Canada and the men in our armed services that we think more of the sacrifices they are making than to allow any laxity in administration, and through not paying attention to even small things. We should not allow, as it says here, a handful of crooks to do what has been done.
Let me repeat what I said in the beginning, that if there is any further information required in connection with this matter, it should not be referred to the committee to be set up on defence expenditures, because that is just the way not to find out what is going on. I have been here long enough and I have been on enough committees to know that the government majority on a committee, if they can prevent it-and there are fairly astute people on committees, including lawyers and others who are adept at covering up-will not let these things come to light. Things should come to light, if they are there.
I would suggest that if this matter does go to the committee on defence expenditures that is to be set up, the chairman of that committee, whoever he may be, should say, "Gentlemen, the lid is off. If there is anything here that should be exposed, then we are going to expose it, regardless of who is going to get hurt in the process". That is the only way in which honest, efficient and democratic government can be carried on.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to join other hon.

members in extending my best wishes to Hon. Robert Mayhew, former minister of fisheries, who comes from British Columbia and who has now taken on a new task as the representative of Canada in Japan. He goes to this task after a long and distinguished career, and I am sure he will acquit himself with distinction in this new field.
I am particularly pleased that, finally, the government has recognized the stature of British Columbia by having seen fit to appoint two cabinet ministers from that province. I am pleased to note that the Prime Minister has chosen two men of proven ability to fill these two important posts. I would say to him and to his colleagues in the cabinet that they would do well if, very often, they were to listen to the sage advice of these two ministers. I might say, too, that British Columbia may now expect the completion of many of the things that have long been deferred. Perhaps with the persuasive eloquence of these two hon. gentlemen something will come to pass.
In passing I should like to make only one or two comments about private television. It seems to me that the government's policy in television is somewhat akin to its policy in respect of Trans-Canada Air Lines. I would like to be able to say that I thought the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has been operated as well as Trans-Canada Air Lines; but I can say that there is a parallel in these two organizations in the fact that both retain for themselves any plums to be found in the business life of Canada, and they allow private aeroplanes or, as in this instance, private television to take the scraps that are left. Sometimes these scraps are in very doubtful spheres, so far as economics are concerned.
I would sincerely like to see the government give one private station out in Vancouver an opportunity to come in and begin to operate now. I have had the assurance from a man interested in putting his money into this field of enterprise that he could have television for Vancouver within six months. If that is so I would like to see the minister give that gentleman the opportunity to do so.
I would say also to the British Columbia cabinet ministers that I would like to have them prevail upon their colleagues to see to it that the committee on veterans affairs is set up again when we return after the Christmas recess, so that we may give careful consideration to the representations made in the brief submitted to us by the Canadian Legion.
Then I should like to speak for a moment or two regarding our highway on Vancouver
The Address-Mr. Gibson island. I hate being parochial at a time like this, when there are so many grave problems before the House of Commons, but I think in this instance Vancouver island has been badly neglected. By some curious circumstance the trans-Canada highway goes to Vancouver, then jumps to Nanaimo, and then proceeds east to Victoria. Just how they arrived at the conclusion that Victoria should be the terminus of the trans-Canada highway, I cannot say. But I would ask the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) to consult with the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) and the new members of the government from British Columbia, to see if we cannot have the trans-Canada highway go from Vancouver to Victoria, and thence due west to the head of Vancouver island.
Sometimes I hear my friends from Prince Edward Island being very sensitive about things that happen there. But if any of them ever wandered so far from home as to see the tremendous island we have out on the western coast, I am sure they would be impressed. I would recall what was said by Kipling many years ago, when he described our island as the fairest gem in the British crown. It is a reflection on Canada and on the trans-Canada highway policy when one cannot travel from one end of Vancouver island to the other. I would ask the responsible minister to consult with the government of British Columbia with a view to rectifying this very serious situation.
There is another highway on Vancouver island about which I have spoken before. I am happy that one of the ministers from British Columbia is to be the associate minister of national defence (Mr. Campney). I am referring now, of course, to the proposed highway from Port Alberni to Tofino airport. It is not generally known that far out on the west coast of Vancouver island we have one of the finest airports in Canada. This was one of the first airports opened during the war for the defence of the west coast. I pointed out last year when I dealt with this matter that there is no access by road to this point. The federal government have always contended that they are not interested in roads and should not participate in the building of roads, but this is the most westerly outpost of our air defences in Canada, and it is not connected by highway. As a matter of fact I can tell the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) that this proved of great disadvantage during the last war. I am quite sure the fact that there was not a road in there cost us far more than it would have cost to construct a road.

I come now to the subject that was covered very ably last night by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Garson). I should like to make some comments with regard to government policy in connection with budget surpluses. The other day the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) pointed this up very dramatically when he said that since 1945 the government has had an average surplus of $1 million per day. That figure is startling.
At the outset of my comments in this regard I should like to pay a sincere personal tribute to our very efficient Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). I must say that I have always admired his courage in imposing these high taxes. I agree with him that they have been a deterring factor in controlling inflation. I think in that aspect he did a good job. I was glad to see him resist over the years the pressure that came from various parts of this house to impose controls on both prices and wages. If we are fair about it I think we would all say that in the long run he has proved to be right, because actually the cost of living is coming down and I think the inflationary trend is lessening.
But I think now with seven years of surpluses we have had about enough. There is no particular virtue in having a surplus all the time, despite the idea of some people that a surplus is always necessary. I think


this is the time for a really healthy deficit. If I were the leader of a large group, instead of being an independent as I am, I think I would suggest that this would be a sound time to use up some of this surplus.
I often wonder whether we Canadians are not becoming a little soft. I know there is a saying that a rich man cannot get into heaven any easier than he can pass through the eye of a needle. I sometimes feel that with all the approbation we have been receiving in the United States press and the press of other countries we have gone perhaps a little too far with the surpluses we are having. Our premium dollar and other things of that kind seem to have gone to our heads. I think we would make better friends for ourselves throughout the world if we played a role that was a little bit poorer, and did not appear to ostentatiously have too much money.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made a statement the other day that rather intrigued me. He said that after all these surpluses are great stuff; and incidentally, I very seldom disagree with him. He told us that these surpluses are good things and that our grandchildren will rise up and call us blessed for not leaving them too much money to pay back. That may be true, but I think as we look back to our youth we must admit that things today are infinitely better than they were when we were young. If the trend continues, then we can expect that things will get progressively better. I contend that our grandchildren will not have too heavy a load to carry even though we do not struggle to pay off all our debt at the present time. I notice that the carpenters of British Columbia are thinking of a 30-hour week, which would seem to indicate that no one is going to have too heavy a burden to carry.
I think Mr. Ilsley did a very good job during the war when he paid half the cost of it from taxation as we went along. We must all agree that he pursued a wise course in that regard. Then as far as the balance is concerned, I think we have made a good job of paying off half of that because of the effects of inflation and the fact that today our dollar is worth only fifty cents compared to what it used to be worth. The present per capita debt is nothing to become alarmed about. In fact I think it could be increased some. Every time the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) brings in 12,000 or 15,000 people in a month we reduce that per capita debt quite substantially. Then when we consider the desirable birth rate we have in this country we must realize that that also is playing a part in reducing the per capita debt.

Canada has so many frontiers to be developed, and when we have surpluses of this kind I think we should look around to see where it can be invested so that the frontiers can be pushed back. After all, money at 3 per cent is pretty cheap money. It is the cheapest money anybody can get. I do not think we ought to strain ourselves at the present time after having reduced our national debt every year for seven years. We do not need to concentrate on reducing it any more at the present time.
Sometimes it is nice to be able to agree with a C.C.F. member like my good friend the hon. member for Moose Jaw. He says taxes are too high. If I remember correctly, he did not say all taxes are too high. He did not say anything about personal income tax, but he did say that the corporation income taxes are too high. I gather that he has some knowledge on that subject. It does not seem right to me that our government should own 52 per cent of every successful incorporated business in Canada; and I do not think they should overtax corporations and individuals to the extent of $1 million a day in order to pay off a debt on which we have to pay only 3 per cent. I think if the average businessman could get all the money he wanted at 3 per cent, he could pay that rate of interest and use the money for expansion of his business and probably make 10 per cent on it.
Once you give money to a government it just goes down the sink, and I would say that of any government. The moment we are able to show up here with a surplus my good friends away down to the left dredge up some brand new idea to get rid of it. And are they efficient at that type of thing!
I have a few suggestions to make, though I hate to make them in an election year. Perhaps I should save them for another year. I will say that I am not speaking with any correct knowledge of that event, so the opposition need not take what I say as an announcement of when the election will be. It seems to me that we have accumulated quite a lot of money, and we should look around to see how we can invest it wisely.
I have dealt with some of the things, and other speakers from British Columbia have mentioned how money might well be spent in the greater Vancouver area. I have mentioned some things that might be done on Vancouver island. However, I must commend the government-and I suppose it is as a result of the surpluses they have had- in that they now find they are able to say that Canada will go ahead on its own and build the St. Lawrence seaway. Coming from the west I know that in a parochial sense
The Address-Mr. Gibson it probably will not do my riding any particular good, but I have always thought anything that is in the interests of Canada, such as the St. Lawrence seaway, is actually of benefit to us all.
The other day the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray) mentioned that it might be a good thing to put some hard surfacing on the Alaska highway. I would commend that to the government as a good place to spend some money. I think a railroad is needed into the Peace river district. I am sure any hon. members who have been in that vast territory will realize what an empire it is and how much it needs opening up and development. There are millions of acres in the Peace river district, and agriculturalists tell me it is the finest land in Canada. When we bring immigrants into this country we tell them there are millions of acres of the finest land in Canada there and that they should go there and settle, but that is most difficult for anybody coming into the country, particularly as these people almost never have a large amount of capital when they come here. It is very difficult for them to go and open up country of that kind. It seems to me that it would demonstrate real vision if the government would go in there and as an experiment clear a million acres of land. I believe that could be done for around $35 million. I think it would be a good test plot, as it were, and that the government would be well advised to undertake a job of that kind to indicate to the people that they have vision and that they have the idea that this country must be opened up. So many people in Canada live in cities, and somehow or other they get the idea that is where the wealth is. That is not true. There is only one place from which wealth comes and that is from our forests, mines, farms and fisheries. The people who live outside the confines of the cities should receive credit for developing this wealth. I should like to see the government give them every possible encouragement.
There is another thing about which I have always been very sorry. I think hon. members will recall that when the pipe-line bills were going through the house in 1949 I suggested that perhaps it would be feasible for the Canadian National Railways to get into the transportation of oil. I pointed out at that time that perhaps the best freight revenue the Canadian National Railways will ever get out of that country is from the transportation of oil. However, I suppose the directors of the C.N.R. were probably too busy wondering about inside plumbing at Riviere du Loup or about what brand of paper cups they were going to use on the trains. They certainly missed the boat. When I
880	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Gibson think of these oil transmission line companies and the way such investments have appreciated on the stock exchange to three or four times their original worth in some cases, I believe we should have been able to advance $300 million to the Canadian National Railways for such a project. We have advanced them hundreds of millions since for other projects. If they had had the necessary vision at that time and had invested $300 million in this way they could perhaps have paid for their own capital reconstruction which we put through the house last year. To me it is a tragedy that they did not have the vision at that time to see what a chance they had. They may have missed the boat in that particular instance, but I would hope that in the future they will not make the same error.
I now want to make a few remarks with respect to the meeting of the commonwealth prime ministers in the old country. I realize we are going to have a debate on this matter later, but I am wondering if we could not have used a little vision there so far as our surpluses are concerned. I realize I am not an international financier. I have never studied economics in a university or anything of that kind, but it has always seemed to me that international and public finance are not too different from private finance. When business is slack in a country; when a manufacturer finds that he has a surplus of goods and that a particular customer is hard up and cannot afford to stock the goods on his shelves, the manufacturer goes to his bank where his credit is good and arranges for credit. He goes to the retailer and says to him, "I will put a stock of my goods on your shelves on a consignment basis. You need goods so you can carry on your business.
I will supply you with the goods, because I have the goods and I have the credit." Is that not just about the position in which Canada is so far as the United Kingdom is concerned? Not only would this be an extremely good move so far as the business aspect of the matter is concerned, but it has always seemed to me that we have been missing the boat strategically so far as the old country is concerned.
I do not like to say it, but I have seen many times in many magazines that in effect the United Kingdom is in great measure our primary outpost of defence. It has been called our unshakable aircraft carrier off the coast of Europe. If it is valid for us to continue to stockpile men and aeroplanes over there, to stockpile guns and equipment, then I submit it should be equally valid for us to make sure that we have a supply of goods over 

there that would be available in the event of war. Nobody wants war, but if it comes we are going to find the same situation that we had the last time. We will find that half the material we send over there in the first year of war will be lost through submarine action. There is no question about that. I suggest to the government that we look at this matter very carefully. As I say, we have many products that we could send over there. I can assure the government that there is lots of lumber and base metals in British Columbia for which we are looking for markets, and I can certainly assure them that there is plenty of canned salmon which would be an excellent product to stockpile in England.
Incidentally, one of the reasons the United Kingdom is short of dollars now for the carrying on of these purchases is the fact that they have had to stockpile. The fact that they did stockpile and then found themselves short of money has caused serious repercussions so far as the base metal mines are concerned, because they will fall short of money to purchase other things. These people say that the cold war does not look quite so hot or cold, and they say they might as well put these stockpiles on the market. As a result we have had tremendous fluctuations in the prices of base metals with very disastrous results to the base metal mines of British Columbia.
I would remind the cabinet-and they must be quite conscious of it-that we have a major shareholder's interest in all the primary industries of this country. So far as canned pork is concerned, I can assure my farmer friends that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has been doing a consistently good job in taking care not only of the pork producers but of the pork packers. They also did very well. It seems to me, however, when the same problem is presented with respect to the salmon industry in British Columbia the government more or less-I do not want to be unkind to them-yawn over that one. The British Columbia salmon industry this year-and I speak not only for the packers but for the fishermen-has had a very difficult time. The country is the senior shareholder in the salmon canneries and in the fishermen and their boats, and I would point out that the industry has lost millions of dollars in British Columbia this year. The industry not only lost 48 per cent of it; the government lost its 52 per cent, and I am quite sure that the returns of the Department of Finance from British Columbia this year will reflect that very serious situation.

So far as stockpiling is concerned, I should like to point out that salmon is something like scotch whisky. You can keep it for twenty years and it is better then than it was when you first bought it. As an old expert who knows what he is talking about as far as canned salmon is concerned, I offer that by way of comment.
If you will forgive me, Mr. Speaker, should I break a rule of the house, I want to talk about practical politics a little. I want to say to the cabinet and to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) that we are not all crazy in British Columbia, despite what happened in the last provincial election. The folks out there are pretty sound, and I would say that 95 per cent do not like, and do not understand this Social Credit monetary theory; and people do not usually support things they do not understand. I will make another categorical statement and say that 75 per cent of them do not want to have anything to do with socialism.
I know the two ministers from British Columbia will give you sound and honest advice. If you listen carefully to what they have to tell you I do not think you will have too much difficulty in British Columbia in the next federal election.
